_README: Approach variants — GLACIER PEAK / CHIWAWA / ENTIAT, Washington, 2026-08-19. 27 routes, 29 variants, every one carrying a baseFinding.
`area` on every entry was READ FROM THE LIVE ROW (routes.area_id), not typed from the route name. Four ids in this
batch carry no peak name at all — wa_soviet_route and wa_don_t_climb_that_she_said, wa_borrowed_time and
wa_superalpine. The first is BONANZA PEAK, the second is filed under GLACIER PEAK, and the last two are SLOAN
PEAK. A name-shaped id is not evidence of which mountain you are on; every one of these was resolved by reading
area_id off the row.
SCOPE was the 23 peaks named in the request. Every one exists in the catalog except that WHITE CHUCK MOUNTAIN
(wa_white_chuck_mountain, filed as a crag under Glacier Peak Wilderness) holds ZERO routes, so there was nothing
to enrich there. Across the other 22 peaks the catalog holds 49 routes, of which 33 had an EMPTY
approach_variants; 27 are written here and 6 were deliberately skipped — see _SKIPPED. The 16 routes that already
carried variants were not touched.
Peaks in the same subtrees but NOT named in the request were left alone, to stay clear of the other agents:
Buckskin, Carne, Cloudy, Dark, Greenwood, Massie, Mount Lyall, North Star, Chalangin, Helmet Butte, Indian Head,
Sitkum Spire, Painted Mountain and Mount Saul all have empty rows and are still available.
CONTAMINATION REJECTED during research, recorded so it is not re-introduced:
- BUCK MOUNTAIN exists twice in Washington. The one in scope is wa_buck_mountain in the Chiwawa Ridge / DaKobed
subtree at 48.0936, -120.9122, reached from Trinity and Buck Creek Pass. The Olympic Buck Mountain is a
different peak in a different range and nothing was carried between them. (That row already had variants and
was not edited; the check was made because Mount Berge's approaches share the Buck Creek trail.)
- MOUNT FERNOW exists twice in Washington — the 9,249 ft Entiat peak (wa_mount_fernow, 48.1625, -120.8074) and
a Wild Sky peak of the same name. Only the Entiat one borders this batch, and only via Leroy Basin, which the
Mount Maude and Seven Fingered Jack rows already describe.
- CLARK MOUNTAIN IS NOT MOUNT CLARK. The Clark in this region is wa_clark_mountain at 48.0500, -120.9686, whose
Walrus Glacier and south-basin routes bound Luahna Peak's approach. Nothing from any Mount Clark was used.
- COPPER PEAK: there is a Copper Peak in Michigan that dominates search results for the name. Every source used
for wa_copper_peak is anchored to Holden Village, Railroad Creek and the Copper Creek boot trail, which no
other Copper Peak has.
- GLACIER PEAK, KENNEDY, WHITE CHUCK and BOULDER are all names that recur across this state and beyond. The
Kennedy in this batch is the glacier on Glacier Peak's north-west flank; the Boulder Creek used for Luahna is
the White River one, NOT the Boulder Creek on Mount Baker that serves the Boulder Glacier routes. Both
catalogs contain a 'Boulder Basin' and they are 100 km apart.
- 'NORTH RIDGE' and 'WEST RIDGE' as route names identify nothing. wa_bonanza_peak_north_ridge carries a beta
field that begins 'From the Middle Fork Snoqualmie trailhead' — a valley on the far side of the Cascade crest
with no connection to Bonanza Peak. That row was SKIPPED rather than repaired; see _DEFECTS.
NO TIME, DISTANCE OR GAIN FIGURE IS WRITTEN IN THIS BATCH. Not one variant carries hours, distMi or gainFt. That
is a finding rather than an omission: on essentially every route here the published figures disagree with the
row's own columns, with each other, or mix one-way and round-trip conventions — Kololo's approach prose cites a
46.99 km round trip against a dist_km of 22.9; Fortress's two rows both record more loss than gain on an
out-and-back; Luahna's two rows differ by 3,250 ft of gain for the same summit from the same trailhead. Averaging
any of that would manufacture a number nobody published.
_confidence values used here: 'corroborated' (two or more independent published sources agree on the base),
'single-source' (one published source plus the route row's own columns), 're-homed' (the material comes from the
route row's OWN approach / climbing_route / descent_text / waypoint prose and no external source was retrieved —
nothing was researched into these, and no source is claimed), and 'thin' (the base is real but under-published;
the entry says so in its own notes).
Every URL in a _sources list was actually retrieved during this pass. Nothing was pattern-guessed. Where a base
finding is re-homed from the row's own columns the _sources list is EMPTY, which is the honest answer rather than
a plausible-looking citation.

approach_variants.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the Glacier Creek camps
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, and it is one of the shorter windows on the mountain — the upper Kennedy is a small, steep glacier that opens into a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses as the season runs on
approach_variants.notes:
The historic line starts at the White Chuck River Trailhead at the end of FR-23 and follows Trail #643 about four miles, then Kennedy Ridge Trail #639 for 1.7 miles to the Pacific Crest Trail near 5,000 ft. Turn north on the PCT and follow it about two miles to the Glacier Creek crossing, where there are established camps with reliable water near 5,300 ft. Four to five hours is the usual pack-in.

FR-23 has been closed from milepost 3.7 to its end, so the reliably open option in recent seasons has been the North Fork Sauk Trail and the PCT over Red Pass to the same Glacier Creek camps. That is a much longer walk to the same place, and it changes nothing above camp.

From the Glacier Creek camp a climbers' trail runs up a gully to the crest of Kennedy Ridge. Everything above is glacier, and the character of the day is set by how well you read the upper glacier rather than by any technical difficulty — the headwall at the top is about 40 degrees and short, while the crevasse field below it is the part parties spend hours on.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START OF THE CLIMB IS BELOW YOU, NOT ABOVE YOU, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE TEST. From the Glacier Creek camp the climbers' trail climbs a gully to the CREST of Kennedy Ridge — and then you go DOWN off the far side, to climber's right, to the foot of the Kennedy Glacier. A party that tops the ridge and keeps climbing has left the route. If you have not lost height since the ridge crest, you have not reached the base.

ARRIVAL: the foot of the glacier, where ridge ground runs out into ice. Rope up there. On the lower glacier keep RIGHT; on the upper glacier take the CENTRE. That right-then-centre sequence is worth memorising before you leave camp, because the upper Kennedy is a maze and there is nothing to sight on inside it.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST FROSTBITE RIDGE, which shares this mountain flank and this camp: Frostbite rounds Kennedy Peak to the saddle between the VISTA and KENNEDY glaciers at about 8,000 ft, climbs the Kennedy to a saddle at about 8,800 ft, and then leaves the ice for the RIDGE. This route never leaves the ice. If you are standing on a saddle looking for a rock crest to follow, you are on Frostbite. If you are still roped on glacier at 9,500 ft heading for a bergschrund, you are on this one.

THE TOP END, AND IT IS A REAL DECISION POINT: the bergschrund sits at the head of the glacier. Reach it by climbing LEFT to the top of a snow dome and looking for a bridge from there — do not walk the schrund's length hunting for a gap at its lowest point. Above it the headwall runs about 40 degrees; stay LEFT of, but close to, the prominent rock outcrops, and that puts you on the crater rim.

WHAT HUGGING THE LEFT WALL COSTS: parties commonly move under the Kennedy Peak wall on climber's left to simplify the crevasse problem. It works, and it buys the simplification with rockfall and serac exposure. That is a trade to make deliberately, not one to drift into.
hazards: An upper glacier described by parties as a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses that needs deliberate, slow routefinding
Seracs on climber's left beneath the Kennedy Peak wall, where some parties have had to belay off bare glacier ice
Trading crevasse navigation for rockfall by hugging the left wall — the simplification is real and so is the cost
A bergschrund at the head of the glacier whose only crossing may be a single bridge found from the snow dome above it
8,200 ft of gain from a trailhead served by a road that has been closed at milepost 3.7, so the walk in may be far longer than the mileage on file

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk Trail #649 to White Pass, then the Foam Basin traverse and the White Chuck Glacier
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Late summer opens the crevasses so you can see and weave them; early season covers them with bridges you cannot read, and puts Red Creek and Lightning Creek in flood
approach_variants.notes:
From the North Fork Sauk Trailhead near 2,050 ft at the end of FR-49, Trail #649 runs about 5.5 miles up the valley on an easy grade through old growth, fording several tributaries. Red Creek is the first crossing that can actually stop you: manageable at normal flow, considerably higher during snowmelt or after rain, and worth a pole. Mackinaw Shelter at 2,950 ft is a possible camp but tight for a big party, and it is where the trail leaves the river — fill water there.

Above the shelter the trail climbs about 3.2 miles of sustained switchbacks to a meadow junction with the Pacific Crest Trail near 6,000 ft, then a quarter mile north on the PCT to White Pass at 5,900 ft. That is roughly nine miles and 4,800 ft from the car and the last easy water before the high traverse.

Maintained trail ends at the pass. Traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin and White River Meadows around 6,300-6,500 ft — the usual base camp — either by way of Red Pass or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck basin.

Almost nobody does this from the car in a day, and the round trip is long enough that the two published distances for it disagree; see _DEFECTS.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE HAS TWO ARRIVALS AND THEY ARE DIFFERENT KINDS OF THING. The first is where GLACIER TRAVEL starts, and the second is where the SCRAMBLING starts. Confusing them is how a party ends up unroped in the wrong place.

GLACIER STARTS AT FOAM PASS. From camp climb to Foam Pass and step onto the White Chuck Glacier. Rope, axe and crampons go on here, not later — the crossing to Glacier Gap and then onto the White River Glacier is the whole of the day's crevasse exposure.

SCRAMBLING STARTS AT THE 7,400 FT SADDLE, AND YOU GET THERE BY COUNTING RATHER THAN BY LOOKING. Off the glacier, gain the flat shoulder near 6,000 ft; follow the connecting ridge north-north-west over a bulge at 7,200 ft; cross the small basin below the east summit; then go WEST a quarter mile to a saddle at 7,400 ft. Shoulder, bulge, basin, saddle — four things in that order. If you have gone west without first crossing a basin, you are on the wrong side of the bulge.

THE ARRIVAL TEST AT THE SADDLE: from it, one ridge runs away from you forming the EAST EDGE OF THE WHITE RIVER GLACIER CIRQUE. That ridge is the route. If the ground ahead does not have a glacier cirque falling away on one side of it, you are not on the saddle you want.

WHAT TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing east instead of west from the 7,200 ft bulge takes you to the EAST summit rather than the summit ridge — and this peak's own record does not agree on which of its two tops is higher, so bagging one of them is not proof of anything. See _DEFECTS before you decide you are done.

ONE THING TO EXPECT ON THE ICE RATHER THAN LOOK FOR: a roughly 200-yard band of exposed blue ice, a shallow icefall, on the White River Glacier. It is a crampon problem, not a navigation one, but it is the reason the descent takes longer than the map suggests.
hazards: Open crevasses and a roughly 200-yard band of exposed blue ice on the White River Glacier, worse late season
Red Creek and Lightning Creek run high and fast in snowmelt — the first is an ordinary ford at normal flow and a stopper at high water
Twelve-plus miles one way with the last several off any maintained trail, so a navigation error is measured in hours
Snow bridges over the White Chuck Glacier that are unreadable under early-season cover
Road closures on FR-49 and the Mountain Loop Highway that can shut the west approach entirely, turning this into a much longer trip from the east

approach_variants.name: White River Trail #1507 and the old sheep path into Thunder Basin
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, while the snow between camp and the col is still continuous enough to walk and the summit rock is dry
approach_variants.notes:
From Coles Corner take Hwy 207 toward Lake Wenatchee, then White River Road (FR-6400) to its end at the White River / Indian Creek Trailhead near 2,300 ft. Hike White River Trail #1507 about six miles to the Thunder Creek crossing; there is an established camp right at the crossing.

Half a mile past Thunder Creek the maintained trail is left behind for an old, unmaintained sheep path that climbs the WEST side of the Thunder Creek drainage. This is the hard part of the walk in: avalanche debris, blowdown, and dense slide alder choking the tread up to about 5,000 ft. Above the alder it opens into a lower basin near 4,175 ft and then climbs steeply into Thunder Basin, an open basin of granite slabs and small tarns which is the standard high camp and has a direct view of the peak.

The row carries three different elevations for that camp; see _DEFECTS. Camp on the slabs by the tarns rather than at a number.

A far longer alternative comes in from the west — North Fork Sauk Trail #649 past Mackinaw Shelter to the PCT, then cross-country over Boulder Pass and through the Napeequa to the peak's north and north-east side. Parties who have done it report twenty-plus stream crossings and heavy brush over three days. It is a different trip, not a shortcut.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL EAST OF THE SUMMIT BLOCK IS THE BASE, AND THE THING THAT CONFIRMS IT IS THE WIND. Parties who have stood there describe it as an incredibly windy notch below the east face — it is a gap on a ridge, so it funnels, and on a Cascade summit day you will feel it before you can see anything.

GETTING THERE IS A SINGLE BEARING FROM CAMP: from Thunder Basin cross talus and snow toward the col that sits EAST of the summit block, near 8,000 ft. Crampons and an axe are normal for the snow, which stays firm in the morning. You are aiming for the gap beside the summit tower, not for the tower.

THE POSITIVE TEST FOR THE START OF THE CLIMBING: from the col the route takes a LOOSE GULLY ON THE LEFT for about 85 ft to a ledge system. Loose first, ledge second. If the first thing above the col is clean solid rock, or if you are moving right rather than left, you are not on it.

THE SECOND CONFIRMATION IS A CRACK. Above the ledge system the finish is a broken chimney with a good jam crack running up it, and that crack is the one genuinely positive hold-bearing feature on the summit block. Class 4 to easy fifth depending on conditions. If you are on a face with no chimney and no crack, you have drifted off the ledge system.

WHAT IT IS NOT: this is a short summit block, not a wall. From the col to the top is roughly two rope lengths. If you have been climbing for hours above the col you are not on this route.

RACK AND ROCK: everything from the col up is loose. Helmet, and space the party out — the gully drops what the leader pulls straight onto whoever is below.
hazards: Loose, rotten rock in the summit gully and the broken chimney above it, directly over anyone belaying below
Dense slide alder choking the old sheep path to about 5,000 ft — the slowest half-mile of the approach by a wide margin
Crevasses on the small hanging glaciers crossed on the northern approach variations
Cornices and wind-loaded slopes on the approach ridgelines into early summer
White River Road has a repeated history of flash-flood washouts, so the drive is the first thing to verify

approach_variants.name: Over the col west of Tenpeak and down the Honeycomb Glacier to the couloir's base
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr-Jul. This is a spring line: it wants continuous firm snow, and it has been climbed and skied as early as mid-April and as late as mid-July. By mid-summer the apron melts out and the couloir bakes to bare ice and scree
approach_variants.notes:
There is no short way to this side of the mountain. Parties reach it either from the White River Trailhead by way of the PCT and the upper White Chuck and Suiattle basins, or by dropping onto the Honeycomb from a high camp out on the Kololo Peaks — which is why it is most often climbed as one leg of a multi-day traverse rather than as an objective on its own.

Either way the ground you cover on the day is the same: reach the col that sits immediately WEST of Tenpeak, cross onto the Honeycomb Glacier there, and lose height across the glacier before traversing in beneath the north side.

The couloir itself is roughly 1,200 ft of snow up to about 35 degrees — a boot-and-axe climb rather than a technical one — finishing on the north-west ridge, where a single short rock pitch of about 5.4 leads to the summit. That last pitch is the reason to carry a rope on a route that otherwise does not obviously need one.

This is the thinnest-documented line in this batch. What is written here comes from a small number of accounts and the route's own row; treat the couloir's condition as unknown until you can see it.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARRIVE AT THIS ROUTE BY GOING DOWN, AND THAT IS THE TEST THAT SEPARATES IT FROM EVERY OTHER LINE ON THE PEAK. Cross the col WEST of Tenpeak onto the Honeycomb Glacier and then LOSE over a thousand feet down the glacier. If you crossed the col and immediately started climbing again, you are on the wrong side of the mountain and probably on the standard south-east line's ground.

THE HANDRAIL IS THE GLACIER AND THE MARKER IS A KNOLL. After the descent, climb to a small knoll and traverse from it into the foot of the couloir. The traverse is easy ground; the knoll is the point you leave the glacier proper. In cloud, the sequence is col, then descent, then one short rise, then a level traverse — four changes of direction, in that order.

WHAT THE BASE LOOKS LIKE, AND THE SEASONAL TRAP THAT COMES WITH IT: early in the season the couloir runs out into a continuous snow apron and you simply walk onto it. By mid-July that apron has melted and the snow starts higher, above bare ground — so a late party finds a gap between the glacier and the climb that an April party never sees. Do not read a missing apron as being in the wrong place.

THE CONFIRMATION ONCE YOU ARE ON IT: about 1,200 ft of sustained snow at up to roughly 35 degrees, no steeper. If the ground stands up beyond that, or if you are on ice and rock rather than snow, you are either in the wrong gully or you are here too late in the year.

THE TOP-OUT IS NOT THE SUMMIT. The couloir finishes on the north-west ridge and there is still one short rock pitch, about 5.4, above it. A party that tops out and starts walking has stopped one pitch short.
hazards: A committing position — once in the couloir the bailout is back down 1,200 ft of snow onto a glacier, hours from anywhere
Rockfall out of the cliff bands flanking the couloir, worse as the day warms
Crevasses on the Honeycomb and the upper Suiattle basins, crossed on the way in and again on the way out
A short rock pitch at the very top that a party carrying no rope cannot protect
Lightning exposure on wholly open upper-mountain terrain with no shelter for miles

approach_variants.name: Mt. Pugh Trail #644 from FR-2095 to Stujack Pass
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-Jul-Oct. Before mid-July the permanent snowfield beside the upper ridge is the crux of the day and wants an axe; October is quiet and superb but the daylight runs short for a 5,300 ft climb
approach_variants.notes:
From Darrington, follow the Mountain Loop Highway south for roughly 12.5 to 14 miles — the sources differ — to a prominent Mount Pugh sign where FR-2095 branches left. It is narrow, one-lane and unpaved; the signed trailhead is on the right at the second switchback near 1,900 ft. Parking is a handful of cars, and the large pullout at the switchback below is the reliable overflow. Note that FR-2095 is gated 16 October to 1 June for wildlife, on top of any Mountain Loop Highway winter closure.

Trail #644 climbs about 1.5 miles through old growth with several stream crossings to Lake Metan near 3,200 ft. That is the LAST RELIABLE WATER on the route — everything above is dry and fully sun-exposed, so tank up there.

Above the lake the trail rounds the north side and switchbacks hard up steep forest, breaking into an open boulder basin near 4,900 ft, and tops out at Stujack Pass at 5,700 ft after about 4.5 miles.

This is one of the largest elevation gains of any maintained Washington trail that reaches a true summit, and the trail is an old fire-lookout line that is eroding and sloughing in places.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
STUJACK PASS IS THE BASE, AND IT IS THE ONE PLACE ON THIS MOUNTAIN YOU CANNOT MISTAKE IN CLOUD: it is where the MAINTAINED TRAIL STOPS. Up to there you have graded tread and switchbacks under your feet; above it you have a rough climbers' path on heather and then blasted ledges on a crest. If you are still walking on built trail, you have not reached the pass. It also marks the Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary.

WHAT HAPPENS IMMEDIATELY ABOVE IT, so you can confirm it from the other side: the path climbs LEFT out of the notch onto heather, contours the EAST side of the ridge, and crosses the head of a small permanent snowfield. Left, then east side, then snow. A path that stays on the crest straight out of the pass is not the route.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS ABOUT CAIRNS, AND IT HAS HURT PEOPLE HERE. Multiple parties warn against following whatever cairn appears next: stray cairns on this mountain lead toward vertical cliff bands that then need unplanned Class 4 downclimbing to escape. Several boot paths braid the upper ridge and they are NOT all equal. Pick the line that keeps the crest or the blasted ledges under you; do not let a rock pile choose for you.

THE HANDRAIL ABOVE THE PASS IS THE CREST ITSELF — a razorback with drops on both sides, skirting the head of a small glacier. It is only Class 2-3, and the consequence of a slip is out of all proportion to that grade. There is an iron ring on the short chimney section; use it as a handhold, and downclimb that section facing in, because the exposure faces you on the way down and every account says it feels worse descending.

THE SUMMIT IS NOT THE FLAT GROUND. The plateau at the top has a roughly 10 ft boulder at its edge that has to be scrambled to tag the true high point. Standing on the flat is not standing on the summit.
hazards: Stray cairns above Stujack Pass that lead to cliff bands and force unplanned Class 4 downclimbing
A knife-edge crest where the climbing is Class 2-3 and the consequence of a slip is not — two fatal falls are on record on this mountain
A small permanent snowfield beside the upper ridge that holds hard snow early and late in the day
An eroding, sloughing old lookout trail, worst on the meadow and talus switchbacks below the pass
No water above Lake Metan at 1.5 miles, on a fully sun-exposed 5,300 ft climb

approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek to the west face basin, then the central line beneath the dagger
approach_variants.season: Deep winter — the first ascent was 19 January. It needs the west face frozen and the ice formed, which on this aspect means cold, settled weather rather than a date
approach_variants.notes:
From the Bedal Creek Trailhead at the end of FR-4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway near 2,800 ft, follow Bedal Creek Trail #705 up the drainage. FR-4096 is not plowed, so in winter the approach starts lower on the road and is normally skinned; travel eases considerably above about 3,700 ft.

The valley beneath the west face is reached around 5,000 ft. From there this route boots directly up the central weakness of the face to a flat basin below the first ice step, and the first ascent party reached that base at first light after leaving the car in the dark.

The climb is about 1,900 ft, six pitches, and the difficulty is front-loaded and then front-loaded again: WI5 out of the basin, WI4 in a corner, a WI3 gully beneath the dagger, then the M7 crux through overhanging rock on thin gear with three fixed pitons, a blue-ice traverse, and a long snow-and-ice headwall at 45 to 60 degrees to the summit ridge.

THREE WINTER LINES SHARE THIS FACE and the baseFinding below is about telling them apart.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FACE HAS AN OBVIOUS LINE ON THE RIGHT AND THIS IS NOT IT. That single sentence sorts out most of the confusion here. The right-hand side of the west face carries the older, easier ice line; this route is the CENTRAL weakness, left of it. If you have walked to the most obvious continuous flow you can see and started up, you are on the wrong climb and on a much easier one.

THE ARRIVAL IS A FLAT BASIN, NOT A WALL. Boot straight up the central weakness of the face until the ground goes level: there is a flat basin immediately below the first ice step, and that flat is where the route starts. If you are still on a rising slope, you have not got there; if you are already swinging tools, you passed it.

THE FEATURE THAT NAMES THIS ROUTE IS A HANGING DAGGER, AND IT IS WHAT SEPARATES IT FROM THE LINE IT SHARES A START WITH. The lower pitches follow the older central route. That older route CUTS RIGHT to easier ground partway up the big rock band; the dagger hangs DIRECTLY ABOVE the point where it does. So the decision is not made at the base at all — it is made at the rock band, and the rule is: where the tracks go right, this route goes straight up under the dagger. A party that follows the rightward escape has climbed the other route.

THE GRADE IS THE CONFIRMATION. Above the schrund-free basin the first pitch is WI5 and steep. Pitch four is M7 through an overhang on thin gear with three fixed pitons in it — fixed pitons are the one hard physical confirmation on the route. If the hardest thing you have met is WI4 and there is no rock crux, you are on a neighbouring line.

WHAT THE DESCENT MEANS FOR THE START: there is no rappelling this route to get out. You either finish and descend the standard line off the summit with rappels and a lot of downclimbing on sustained 60-degree ground, or you rappel the neighbouring ice line on V-threads. Decide which before you leave the basin, because both cost daylight.
hazards: High-consequence, exposed belay stances the whole way up, with a crux led on thin gear
Solar warming of the west face bringing rockfall and debris onto the upper snow-and-ice headwall
A committing line — the escape is up, or a V-thread rappel descent of a different route
Winter approach on an unplowed road, so a benightment starts hours from the car
The route's condition cannot be judged from the valley; the dagger forms or it does not

approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek on skis to the 5,000 ft meadow, then the right-hand line on the west face
approach_variants.season: Late Nov to mid-Mar, most reliably Jan-Feb when a settled cold spell has let the ice form
approach_variants.notes:
From the Bedal Creek Trailhead on FR-4096 the approach is normally skinned — the road is not plowed, so in a normal winter the skinning starts below the trailhead. Four to five hours gets you into the Bedal Creek valley and the meadow beneath the west face around 5,000 ft. Parties commonly carry on up the spur ridge west of the peak to about 5,700 ft and leave skis there before the technical ground.

The climb is about 1,000 ft: an approach pitch of rambly ice, a solid near-vertical curtain of roughly 25 ft at WI4, then close to 60 m of fat WI3 in the main gully, 100 m and more of easier ground with ice smears through an easy chimney, and a short WI3 step before the upper snowfields.

It was first climbed to the snowfields rather than to the top; the continuation to the summit was done later. Above the ice there are several hundred feet of snowfield left before you are anywhere.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS IS THE OBVIOUS LINE ON THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE FACE, AND "OBVIOUS" IS THE TEST RATHER THAN A FIGURE OF SPEECH. Standing in the meadow beneath the west face, the steep weakness on the RIGHT is the one that reads as a line from a distance. Every other winter route on this face is to its LEFT and none of them look as continuous. If you have walked left of centre looking for something better, you have left this route.

START HEIGHT: about 5,700 ft, gained by climbing the spur ridge west of the peak out of the 5,000 ft meadow. That 700 ft of rise between the meadow and the start is the reason parties leave skis at the top of it — it is where walking stops.

THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE BASE: there are several flows in the bottom of the feature and any of them will get you started; they all lead into ONE ice gully proper. So do not stand and choose. Climb the easiest flow you can reach and expect the ground to funnel — if it does not funnel into a single gully within a rope length or two, you are not on it.

THE CONFIRMATION IS A CURTAIN, AND IT COMES SECOND. The first real difficulty is a solid, roughly 25 ft near-vertical curtain at WI4 above the rambly start, and above that close to a full rope length of fat WI3. Rambly first, curtain second. If your FIRST ground above the snow is steep and hard, you are on one of the harder lines to the left.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER THAT MATTERS MOST: the central weakness left of this route carries lines with a hanging dagger and an overhanging mixed crux on fixed pitons. If you find yourself under a dagger, or looking at fixed pins in overhanging rock, you are on a route two grades harder than the one you came for.

WHERE IT ENDS IS NOT THE TOP. The ice runs out into upper snowfields several hundred feet below the summit. Finishing the ice is not finishing the mountain, and by then the west face has been in the sun.
hazards: Wet loose avalanche on the steep upper snowfields becoming likely by midday
Rockfall and spindrift increasing through the afternoon as the west face warms
A descent choice that must be made in advance — V-threads down the line, or up and over to the standard descent
Unplowed road access, so a slow day ends with a long ski out in the dark
Ice that forms only in settled cold; a warm week can leave the whole feature unclimbable

approach_variants.name: Holden Village to Holden Lake and Holden Pass, then the Mary Green's north margin to the buttress toe
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jun to mid-Jul for the easiest bergschrund and glacier margin; the buttress itself is dry rock and tolerates a later start into August
approach_variants.notes:
There is no road to this trailhead. Drive to Chelan or Field's Point Landing, take the passenger boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, and ride the village bus up to Holden Village near 3,300 ft. The whole trip is gated by a boat and bus timetable rather than by the weather window, so build the itinerary around sailing days. Both the road and the boat shuttle have been closed since the December 2025 flood and landslide — verify access exists before planning anything.

From the village, Railroad Creek Trail #1256 runs about a mile up the valley on near-level grade to a signed fork. Turn RIGHT and climb roughly four miles and 1,700 ft of switchbacks to Holden Lake at about 5,280 ft, the usual first-night camp. Carry water up from the creek — there is none on the switchbacks.

From the head of the lake a climbers' path gains about 1,100 ft over heather benches and rocky terraces to Holden Pass near 6,400 ft. That is effectively the last water; everything above has to be carried.

What makes this route different from the standard line starts at the pass: instead of angling onto the glacier, it stays on benches and talus to climber's RIGHT of it. Expect about three more hours and a lot of gain above the pass, which is why this route's total is so much larger than the standard's.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE GLACIER IS THE HANDRAIL AND THE BUTTRESS TOE IS WHERE IT RUNS OUT. Once you have gained the Mary Green Glacier's northern edge around 7,800 ft, follow the glacier's climber's-RIGHT (north) margin west, then bend south-west along the foot of the north-east ridge to the glacier's upper south-west corner. The rock rib comes down into the ice there, around 8,350 ft. Walk the margin until the ice meets rock; that is the base, and you do not need to see the summit to find it.

HOLDING THE MARGIN IS A TRADE, AND IT IS DELIBERATE: staying on the edge keeps crevasse exposure low and puts you underneath rock the entire way. Helmets on from the moment you start the traverse, not from the moment you start climbing.

GETTING ONTO THE GLACIER IN THE FIRST PLACE — the step most parties get wrong: from Holden Pass make a RISING traverse west along the ridge over benches, talus and heather until a snowfield appears below a band of slabs, then scramble the slabs to the glacier's north edge. There is no single obvious line through the benches, the footing is loose, and it is real routefinding. If you are contouring flat rather than rising, you will end up under the slabs rather than on them.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE STANDARD ROUTE, WHICH LEAVES FROM THE SAME CAMP: the standard line goes UP THE GLACIER and it identifies itself by WATER — low-angle slabs with a waterfall running down them at roughly 7,000 to 7,300 ft. This route never touches those slabs and never crosses the glacier's middle. If you are climbing wet rock beside running water, you are on the standard route.

THE CONFIRMATION ONCE YOU ARE ON IT: the crest steepens and narrows IMMEDIATELY above the toe — several rope lengths of Class 4 and low fifth on and just right of the crest, running into sustained 5.6-5.7 with glacier falling away on both sides. If the ground above the toe stays broken and easy for a long way, you have started up the wrong rib.

WHAT TOO FAR ALONG LOOKS LIKE: the licheny mid-buttress at about 9,000 ft is the sustained section, and from the toe to the summit is roughly four hours on the ridge. Reaching easy fourth-class crest with gendarmes to turn means you are near the top, not near the start.
hazards: Rockfall the whole length of the glacier-margin traverse, because holding the margin puts you under rock rather than over crevasses
Loose, lichen-covered rock on the buttress with sustained 5.6-5.7 and wild exposure to the glacier below
A moat and steep snow crossing near the summit ridge that parties rope even when they scramble everything else
Route-finding through unmarked benches, talus and heather above Holden Pass, on loose footing, with no obvious line
Total dependence on a boat and bus timetable — and both have been closed since the December 2025 flood

approach_variants.name: Railroad Creek Trail to Hart Lake, then the terraces to the North Star-Bonanza col
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Aug into Sep, when the rock is driest
approach_variants.notes:
From Holden Village follow Railroad Creek Trail #1256 WEST up the valley about 3.5 miles to Hart Lake at about 3,956 ft. The Holden Lake Trail branches off partway along and is NOT your turn — stay on the main valley trail the whole way. Hart Lake is the last easy water and the last straightforward walking.

Leave the maintained trail at the lake and fill up, because the ground above holds very little water. Climb out of the lake basin onto the rock-and-heather terraces on the true left (west) side of the drainage, staying LEFT of the waterfalls and cliff bands that come down off the west-facing buttress. Open forest gives way to heather benches and then blocky, loose ground — roughly 3,000 ft of gain, two and a half to three hours, and genuinely routefinding-heavy. There is no trail above Hart Lake.

Camp is the flat ground near the 7,100 ft col between North Star Mountain and Bonanza's Southwest Peak, with snowmelt and tarns for water.

The wall above this camp is one of the largest in the Cascades and carries THREE routes. Telling them apart at the base is what the baseFinding below is for.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE SOVIET IS A CHIMNEY, AND IT IS NOT AT THE LOWEST POINT OF THE BUTTRESS. From camp cross the talus basin to the foot of the buttress — a little under an hour of walking on loose blocks with no trail. The climb starts about 60 FT ABOVE THE LOWEST POINT OF THE TOE, where a narrow chimney takes the first pitch at 5.7. Narrow chimney, 5.7, roughly a rope length: that is the confirmation. If your first pitch is a face, or if it is harder than 5.7, you are not on it.

LEFT TO RIGHT ACROSS THIS WALL, FACING IT FROM THE WEST, THE THREE ROUTES ARE: OREGONIAN, SOVIET, CASCADIAN. Learn that before you leave camp. The Soviet is the MIDDLE one, and the two neighbours identify themselves at the base by things you can see in poor light.

HOW TO KNOW YOU HAVE NOT GONE TOO FAR LEFT: the Oregonian is reached by walking PAST this buttress to the north and crossing the toe of a small POCKET GLACIER. If you have put crampons on, or stepped onto snow to reach rock, you have walked past the Soviet.

HOW TO KNOW YOU HAVE NOT GONE TOO FAR RIGHT: the Cascadian starts on WHITE SLABS beside a small caret-shaped snowpatch, and its opening pitch is an easy 5.4 scramble leading to an obvious large open book. Easy slabby ground and a big corner above means you are one route right of here.

THE ROUTE-FINDING KEY IS HIGH, NOT LOW, AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING FROM THE GROUND: around half height a SLOPING RAMP cuts diagonally across the buttress crest from east to west. That ramp is the whole line — it bypasses two headwalls that block anything direct. Below it there is a cave-like alcove used as a belay by both the first-ascent party and later parties, which is the one comfortable stance on the climb and a reliable position check.

WHAT THE ROCK TELLS YOU: it is meta-granitic and mostly good, with bands of loose RED rock. Below the summit headwall the rock turns visibly redder and looser. Favour solid grey stone where the line allows — where you are on red rock, you are where the route is at its worst, not where you are off it.

THE DESCENT IS NOT A REVERSE. From the Southwest Peak you traverse the north-east ridge to the West Peak over gendarmes with one short rappel, then make two roughly 200 ft rappels down slabs on the north-west side. Anchors there have historically been improvised — a nut and a piton on one recorded descent — so carry cord and rack for them and a rope long enough for 200 ft raps.
hazards: Rockfall from loose reddish rock bands, worst below the summit headwall
Almost no weather escape high on the route on a wall this size
A long descent traverse over a gendarmed ridge followed by two 200 ft rappels off anchors that are not fixed
Route-finding on the terraces above Hart Lake, which has no trail and is loose and brushy enough to be a crux of its own
Extreme remoteness and very few repeat ascents, so nothing about conditions can be inferred from recent traffic

approach_variants.name: The North Star-Bonanza col, then past the Soviet buttress and across the pocket glacier
approach_variants.season: Roughly Aug-Sep; the first ascent was in early September
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the standard one for this side of the peak and is shared with the route next door: Lake Chelan ferry to Lucerne, village bus to Holden, Railroad Creek Trail #1256 west up the valley to Hart Lake at about 3,956 ft, then leave the trail and climb the rock-and-heather terraces on the west side of the drainage to camp near the 7,100 ft col between North Star Mountain and Bonanza's Southwest Peak.

The first-ascent party did not use it — ferry and road closures that year forced them into a roughly 32-mile one-way approach from the west up the Suiattle, including about ten miles of mountain biking, then the PCT to Suiattle Pass, Cloudy Pass and cross-country to the col. That was a workaround, not the route's approach, and it should not be copied unless the boat is out again.

From the top of the col to the first climbing is about an hour and a half of talus and scree.

The route is roughly 2,200 ft with about 1,600 ft of independent ground, sustained 5.6-5.8 with moves to 5.9+, and it joins the route next door for the last 600 ft to the summit block.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU REACH THIS ROUTE BY CROSSING SNOW, AND ITS NEIGHBOUR BY NOT CROSSING ANY. That is the cleanest test on this wall. From the col, traverse north-east PAST the Soviet Route's buttress — about an hour and a half, some of it excellent scree — and then make a rising traverse UP THE TOE OF A SMALL POCKET GLACIER. If you got to rock without touching snow or ice, you stopped one buttress short and you are at the Soviet.

THE EXACT POINT YOU GAIN ROCK: a FEW DOZEN YARDS UPHILL AND LEFT OF THE LOWEST POINT OF THE BUTTRESS, off the top of that pocket-glacier traverse. Not at the toe, and not on the right side.

THE CONFIRMATION IS INSTANT AND IT IS THE STRONGEST THING ON THIS PAGE: you are making NEAR-VERTICAL 5.8-5.9 MOVES IMMEDIATELY, from the first pitch. There is no easing-in. If the climbing above where you stepped onto rock is scrambly, or a chimney, or 5.7, you are on the Soviet buttress instead — that route starts with a narrow chimney 60 ft above its own toe and is a full grade easier out of the blocks.

LEFT TO RIGHT ACROSS THE WALL, FACING IT FROM THE WEST: OREGONIAN, SOVIET, CASCADIAN. This is the LEFT-hand (northern) one, which is why the instruction is always "keep walking".

THE MID-ROUTE CHECKPOINT, which matters because the first ascent bivied there: seven pitches of moderate ground with harder moves, often loose, sparsely protected and lichenous but on the crest of the buttress, lead to a LOWER LEDGE flat enough to sleep on. Above it a near-vertical wall with several significant overhangs rises for more than 600 ft, and the way through is a small ledge system traversing LEFT to regain the crest — that pitch has the best rock on the climb. A party staring up at overhangs and thinking about rappelling is in the right place and looking at the wrong feature.

WHERE IT STOPS BEING ITS OWN ROUTE: the last 600 ft are shared with the Soviet, and the two lines converge at a pinnacle around 8,700 ft before continuing to the Southwest Summit. Meeting another route's ground high up is expected here, not a sign you have wandered.
hazards: Loose, sparsely protected and often lichen-covered rock on a long sustained buttress
A near-vertical 600 ft wall with significant overhangs directly above the bivy ledge, passed only by a small left-trending ledge system
Very few bail options once above the lower ledge, on a wall with no fixed gear
A rising traverse up the toe of a pocket glacier just to reach the rock, in approach shoes for most parties
Total dependence on the Lake Chelan boat and the Holden bus, both closed since the December 2025 flood

approach_variants.name: The North Star-Bonanza col, then talus south to the white slabs beside the caret-shaped snowpatch
approach_variants.season: Roughly Aug-Sep; the only ascent on record is late August, and its two neighbours were also climbed in late summer for the driest rock
approach_variants.notes:
Same approach as its neighbours and the same camp: drive to Chelan, ferry to Lucerne, bus to Holden Village, then about eleven miles of trail and cross-country to a camp near 7,000 ft at the North Star-Bonanza col. It is a full day of travel and approach before anything else happens.

From camp the base is reached over talus. This route is on the WEST FACE proper rather than the north-west buttress its two neighbours share, and it tops out just right of the Southwest Summit.

It is sixteen pitches, just over 2,000 ft of net gain and about 2,800 ft of climbing, with a great deal of loose rock and several pitches where the protection is minimal and the holds are portable. Bail options near the summit roof systems are poor.

The descent from the Southwest Summit traverses to the Isella Glacier and follows an undulating line of steep rock and moraine at about two-thirds of the glacier's height, then crosses a notch in the south ridge back to the col camp — two ropes.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIRST PITCH BEGINS AT A SMALL CARET-SHAPED SNOWPATCH, AND YOU START JUST RIGHT OF IT. That patch is the marker the first-ascent party chose to record, and it is the only thing at the base of this wall that is a shape rather than a description. Walk the talus until you find it.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS A COLOUR CHANGE, AND IT IS EXCELLENT IN BAD LIGHT: pitch one is a 220 ft scramble at about 5.4 up WHITE SLABS to a stance below a large, steeper band of DARKER rock. White below, dark above, easy climbing. If your first pitch is hard, or if the rock is uniform, you are somewhere else.

THE SECOND CONFIRMATION IS ABOVE THE FIRST: from that stance you are aiming for an OBVIOUS, LARGE OPEN BOOK, which takes the second pitch at 5.8. A big open corner directly above easy white slabs is the pair of features that identifies this route. One without the other is not enough.

LEFT TO RIGHT ACROSS THIS WALL, FACING IT FROM THE WEST: OREGONIAN, SOVIET, CASCADIAN. This is the RIGHT-hand one — looker's right of both older routes, which are on the north-west buttress and are out of view at the far left margin of the wall from here. If you can see two other lines to your left and none to your right, you are in the correct place.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE STRONGEST ON THIS PAGE, AND IT IS ABOUT WHAT LIES FURTHER RIGHT: the part of the wall to the right of this route, above the LONG SNOWFIELD, IS UNCLIMBED, and the party who looked hardest at it described it as atrocious. This route begins just right of a TINY snowpatch, not above a long one. If you are standing under a big snowfield, keep walking back left.

WHERE IT EASES: difficulties relent only on reaching the ridge just south of the true summit, sixteen pitches up. There is no midway escape.
hazards: Abundant loose rock over sixteen pitches, with several pitches on minimal protection and portable holds
Poor retreat options near the summit roof systems on a wall with no fixed gear
A descent that crosses the Isella Glacier and a notch in the south ridge, needing two ropes and daylight
Rock quality that varies pitch by pitch, including a choss band low on the route taken at 5.9R
Remoteness on the scale of a three-day weekend before the first pitch, on boat-and-bus access that is currently closed

approach_variants.name: Railroad Creek Trail past the Holden Lake fork to Hart Lake, then the terraces to the 7,100 ft pass
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct; Aug-Sep for the driest ground on the terraces
approach_variants.notes:
This row is the APPROACH to the west side of the peak rather than a climb in its own right — it is how parties reach the base of the routes on the Southwest and West Peaks. Its own beta describes what happens above the pass in terms that nothing else on this mountain supports; see _DEFECTS before you rely on it.

From Holden Village, follow Railroad Creek Trail #1256 west up the valley about 3 to 3.5 miles to Hart Lake at 3,956 ft. Then leave the maintained trail and climb cross-country — roughly two and a half hours, about 3,000 ft — up the rock and heather terraces on the west side of the drainage to the 7,100 ft pass between North Star Mountain and Bonanza's Southwest Peak.

There is no trail above Hart Lake and no reliable water between the lake and the tarns at the pass, so fill at both.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ONE DECISION THAT MATTERS IS MADE ONE MILE FROM THE VILLAGE, AND IT IS A FORK. About a mile up Railroad Creek Trail the Holden Lake Trail branches off. TAKE THE MAIN VALLEY TRAIL, NOT THE FORK. The fork leads to Holden Lake, Holden Pass and the Mary Green Glacier — the routes on the OTHER SIDE of the mountain. Every hour you spend on the wrong branch is an hour walking away from this side of the peak, and the two never rejoin.

THE HANDRAIL IS THE VALLEY AND THE MARKER IS A LAKE. Stay beside Railroad Creek to Hart Lake, at about 3,956 ft, roughly three and a half miles in. Reaching a lake on the valley floor with maintained trail all the way to it means you took the correct branch. Reaching a lake after four miles of switchbacks climbing 1,700 ft out of the valley means you took the wrong one.

ARRIVAL: the flat ground of the 7,100 ft PASS between North Star Mountain and Bonanza's Southwest Peak, with snowmelt and tarns for water. It is a col, so it has ground falling away on two sides, and the wall you came for stands directly above it — under an hour of talus from camp to the foot of the buttress.

THE ROUTE-FINDING RULE ON THE TERRACES, AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE: waterfalls and cliff bands come down off the west-facing buttress. STAY LEFT OF THEM. Open forest gives way to heather benches and then blocky loose ground; there is no tread and no cairned line, so the negative marker is your handrail — if running water or a cliff band is on your left, you have drifted right and need to correct before the ground steepens.

WHAT THIS ROW DOES NOT SETTLE: it describes Class 2-3 scrambling above 8,000 ft on this ridge, and no other account of this peak supports a scramble line there. Treat the pass as the destination and choose a documented route from it, rather than starting up the ridge on the strength of this row.
hazards: Wholly untrailed terraces above Hart Lake with waterfalls and cliff bands to be skirted on the left, loose rock and brush throughout
No reliable water between Hart Lake and the tarns at the pass
Taking the Holden Lake fork by mistake, which commits you to the far side of the mountain
Exposed high camp at 7,100 ft that collects afternoon electrical activity
Boat-and-bus access to Holden Village that has been closed since the December 2025 flood

approach_variants.name: Holden Village to Holden Pass, then east up the ridge
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, with August the most reliable
approach_variants.notes:
Access is by Lake Chelan ferry from Chelan or Field's Point Landing to Lucerne Landing, then the Holden Village shuttle bus up eleven miles of gravel road and twelve switchbacks into the village. Both have been closed since the December 2025 flood; confirm they are running before anything else.

From the village, Railroad Creek Trail #1256 runs a mile up-valley to the fork, then the Holden Lake Trail climbs about four miles and 1,700 ft to Holden Lake at 5,278 ft. Above the lake the climbers' path gains a further 1,100 ft over heather benches and rocky terraces to Holden Pass near 6,400 ft. This is the same camp Bonanza's routes use, and it is effectively the last water.

The rock on this route is loose crumbly schist and marble all the way up, and parties route-find by cairn rather than by feature. There is a fixed rappel anchor near the top for the crux step.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
HOLDEN PASS SERVES TWO MOUNTAINS AND THE DIRECTION YOU LEAVE IT IS THE WHOLE ROUTE-FINDING PROBLEM. The pass is the saddle BETWEEN Bonanza and Martin. Bonanza's routes go WEST from it, onto benches and the Mary Green Glacier. Martin's West Ridge goes EAST, straight up out of the pass. If you are traversing toward a glacier, you are on Bonanza's ground.

SO THE BASE IS THE PASS ITSELF: no approach across a glacier, no basin, no traverse. The ridge rises directly out of the saddle and the scrambling starts where the heather runs out.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS WHICH SIDE OF THE CREST YOU ARE ON, AND IT REPEATS. Gain the ridge by a series of gullies and scramble on the RIGHT — the SOUTH — side of the crest, then repeat that pattern upward. Right side, gully, back toward the crest, right side again. A party on the north flank has left the route, and the north side of this crest is not the easier ground.

IN FOG, FOLLOW CAIRNS HERE RATHER THAN FEATURES. The rock is uniformly crumbly schist and beige marble and one gully looks like the next; on this particular route cairn-following is the documented method rather than a bad habit. That is the opposite of the advice for the scramble on Mount Pugh, where cairns lead to cliffs — do not carry one peak's rule to the other.

THE ARRIVAL AT THE CRUX IS AN ANCHOR, WHICH IS RARE ON THIS MOUNTAIN. About 100 ft below the summit a steep, exposed Class 4 gully is the route's hardest ground, with good holds, and a FIXED RAPPEL ANCHOR has been observed beside it. Finding fixed hardware on this peak means you are 100 ft from the top and on the standard line. Finding none, on ground much harder than Class 4, means you are not.

THE LOOSE BEIGE-MARBLE GULLY partway up is the other named feature and it is on the south side of the crest, so it doubles as a position check: you should meet it while traversing right, not while on the crest.
hazards: Loose, crumbly schist and marble across the entire route, on and off the crest
A short, exposed Class 4 step just below the summit — a fixed anchor is present but is not maintained by anyone
One gully looking exactly like the next on a route where cairns, not features, are the navigation
Sharing a camp with Bonanza parties and a pass with two mountains' worth of routes leaving it in opposite directions
Ferry and shuttle access to Holden Village, closed since the December 2025 flood

approach_variants.name: Holden Village and the Copper Creek boot trail to the Copper Basin bench
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, best in August; the snowfield below the ridge often still wants crampons and an axe into July
approach_variants.notes:
There is no drivable trailhead. Ferry from Chelan or Field's Point to Lucerne, shuttle up to Holden Village near 3,300 ft. Both have been closed since the December 2025 flood and landslide.

From the village, walk the old mine road and Railroad Creek Trail about half a mile east to a large TAILINGS PILE around 3,320 ft, where the Copper Creek Trail branches off on the far side of the creek. A footbridge is the normal crossing; if it is out this becomes a ford and it runs highest in early season.

Above the tailings the boot trail turns steep at once, climbing about 0.7 mile of open burned hillside — loose footing in standing dead timber, unmaintained, slower than its half-mile suggests — before dropping into the Copper Creek drainage. It then parallels the creek south about three miles to an open bench at roughly 5,600 ft, which is the standard camp. Maps show maintained tread ending near 4,750 ft but the boot path continues; do not read the end of the mapped trail as the end of the path.

From camp, ford Copper Creek to its WEST side and climb into the upper basin on talus and slabs, following the outlet stream that drains the glacier remnant on the peak's east face.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A NOTCH, AND IT IS THE BEST NEGATIVE MARKER ON THIS PEAK: SEVERAL NOTCHES CUT THE SPUR RIDGE AND MOST OF THEM ARE CLASS 5 FROM BELOW. The one you want is THE HIGHEST NOTCH YOU CAN REACH EASILY, gained by a loose Class 3-4 gully on climber's RIGHT — the north side — near the top of the glacier. Picking it is the route. If the notch in front of you needs fifth-class moves to enter, it is the wrong notch and there is a better one further up and right.

HOW YOU KNOW YOU ARE UNDER IT: you have crossed the glacier remnant on the east face, roped, and you are near its top. The glacier is a fraction of its mapped size and crevasses are usually minor and walkable around, but the moats along the rock margins are what show themselves late in the summer.

THE STREAM IS THE HANDRAIL FROM CAMP: leave the trail at the bench, ford to the west side, and follow the OUTLET STREAM that drains the glacier. It comes from the thing you are walking to, so in cloud it is a line you can follow uphill without seeing anything.

WHAT HAPPENS IMMEDIATELY AFTER THE NOTCH, so you can confirm you took the right one: turn LEFT and traverse a short, steep snowfield — roughly a hundred feet of exposed side-hilling that usually wants crampons and is worth a belay if the surface has gone hard. Once on the crest, blocky Class 3 leads up the ridge to the summit. Notch, then a hundred feet of side-hill snow, then the crest. If there is no snow traverse beyond the notch, you are in a different one.

THE LAST OBSTACLE IS ONE MOVE, NOT A PITCH. A single short, exposed Class 3+ or 4 step sits just below the top, and some parties carry a short handline for one airy notch there — a fixed handline, not a rappel. If you are looking for rappel anchors on this route you will not find any; nothing on it is rappelled.

A NOTE ON THE ROUTE'S NAME: the row calls this the South Route with a south-east aspect, and everything published about it describes the EAST-facing glacier remnant and the upper NORTH-EAST ridge. See _DEFECTS. Navigate by the glacier and the notch, not by the compass point in the name.
hazards: Several notches in the spur ridge, most of them Class 5 from below — picking the wrong one is the route's real crux
Crevasses and rock-margin moats on the diminished glacier remnant, worst late summer
A short exposed Class 4 step below the summit ridge with no fixed protection
Standing dead timber and loose footing in the burn above the tailings pile
Two creek crossings that both run high in early-season melt, one of them dependent on a footbridge that may be out

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek Trail #1511 to Spider Meadow and upper Phelps Basin
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep. Before that the approach gully and the upper basin are full snow, wanting an axe and often crampons; snow returns to the upper mountain by late September
approach_variants.notes:
From the Phelps Creek Trailhead at about 3,500 ft at the end of FR-6211, follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 north up the EAST side of the creek. It climbs gently — roughly 1,900 ft over five or six miles — through old and second growth, with several small side streams giving reliable water the whole way. After a heavy avalanche winter the tread threads graveyards of downed timber pushed across it from the slopes to the west.

Spider Meadow near 5,150-5,400 ft is the last easy, reliable water. Walk the length of the meadow to its head, where the trail forks. THE FORK IS UNSIGNED: the left branch carries on toward Spider Gap and Larch Knob, and the Dumbell path is the RIGHT-hand one, an old climbers' trail into lower Phelps Basin. Most parties camp in the basin around 5,700 to 6,000 ft.

A longer alternate reaches the same basin from the east over Spider Gap from Railroad Creek and Lyman Lake out of Holden Village — used by parties already doing that loop, not as a way in.

Note that FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which blocks the drive to this trailhead entirely.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE APPROACH TO THE CLIMBING IS A CREEK, AND IT IS THE ONLY WAY THROUGH AN OTHERWISE CLIFFY FACE. From camp in upper Phelps Basin, leave the last of the boot path and head EAST-NORTH-EAST beside a TUMBLING SIDE CREEK. That creek cuts the one weakness in the cliffs above the basin; the broad talus-and-scree gully on Dumbell's south side follows it. If you are working up an open face with no water beside you, you are not in the breach.

THE FIRST ARRIVAL IS A NOTCH ON THE SOUTH-EAST SHOULDER, around 7,900 ft, reached by climbing that gully out of the basin directly south of the summit. Grass and heather give way to talus and — through about mid-August — moderate snow.

THEN COMES THE MEASUREMENT THAT DECIDES THE DAY, AND IT IS COUNTED IN YARDS RATHER THAN LOOKED FOR: FROM THE NOTCH, GO 100 TO 200 YARDS LEFT — WEST — AND TAKE THE GULLY THERE. Not the gully at the notch. Aim for the right-hand side of the south face, where the easiest gully system starts. Several parallel gullies and ledge lines look alike here and they do not all go: the wrong one cliffs you out below the summit ridge.

WHAT CONFIRMS YOU CHOSE RIGHT: a little scrambling above that gully gains a SYSTEM OF LEDGES which then ZIG-ZAGS up onto the WEST RIDGE. Ledges that zig-zag rather than a continuous line, and a ridge crest at the top of them, is the confirmation. A gully that runs out against steeper rock with no ledge system is the wrong one — go back down and try further west.

THE SUMMIT WARNING IS REAL AND IT IS ABOUT LOOKALIKES: from the west ridge a few hundred feet of easy but exposed Class 3 leads to the top, and similar-looking notches and false summits near the top have sent parties astray. Keep track of which top you are on rather than assuming the first one is it.

ONE OBJECT TO KNOW ABOUT: a party has reported an unstable, truck-sized snow block perched on a slab near 8,000 ft in the direct south-face gully. Treat the direct line under it as loaded ground rather than a shortcut.
hazards: Several parallel gullies and ledge systems on the south face that look identical and do not all go — the documented way to get cliffed out here
A reported truck-sized snow block perched on a slab near 8,000 ft in the direct south-face gully
Loose rock and rubble in the gully and on the summit ledges, with parties above you
Lookalike notches and false summits near the top
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which blocks the standard drive entirely

approach_variants.name: Trinity and the Chiwawa River Trail to Chiwawa Basin and the 6,300 ft benches
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Sep. The road to Trinity is often not melted out until mid-June, and the upper mountain and col hold snow into July in heavy years
approach_variants.notes:
Park at Trinity Trailhead near 2,800 ft at the end of Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 by the old mine site. Start up-valley on Buck Creek Trail #1513 for about a mile and a half and BEAR RIGHT at the fork onto Chiwawa River Trail #1550, which takes over an old mining-road grade close to the river — water is reliable along all of this.

About 3.7 more miles brings the signed Red Mountain Trail junction near 4,000 ft. This is the last water that is both obvious and easy to reach before the basin, so fill here. Bear LEFT into Chiwawa Basin rather than taking the right-hand switchbacks up Red Mountain.

Beyond the junction the tread deteriorates, braids and climbs through forest toward the basin, with an unbridged ford of the Chiwawa headwater around 4,400 ft — manageable at summer flow, higher and pushier early. Above the ford the brush thickens and the tread fades: favour the more open, less-timbered ground along the EAST side of the basin, because drifting into the timber turns this into a bushwhack.

Camp is on benches around 6,300 ft. Several lines reach them: the left-trending gully is the most direct and easiest going though it is wet, and the vegetated slopes beside the talus gullies are the better choice coming down.

FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, so Trinity is currently not reachable by vehicle.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A NOTCH IN SOMEBODY ELSE'S RIDGE, AND SAYING IT THAT WAY IS WHAT MAKES IT FINDABLE: the Fortress-Chiwawa col at about 7,200 ft is the NOTCH IN FORTRESS MOUNTAIN'S EAST RIDGE. From the 6,300 ft benches, traverse steep heather and aim for that notch. You are walking toward a gap on the skyline of the mountain NEXT DOOR, not toward the peak you are climbing.

WHAT THE LAST STRETCH FEELS LIKE, so you know you are on it: the snow slope up to the col is moderate and then steepens noticeably in the final section below the notch, and the rock flanking it is loose and sandy. Stay on the snow or on the most solid line you can find rather than the flanking rock. A slope that stays uniformly moderate all the way to a gap is not this one.

FROM THE COL THE ROUTE HAS NO SINGLE LINE AND THAT IS THE CORRECT ANSWER, NOT A GAP IN THE BETA: work up the south-west side on slabs, gullies and talus taking the path of least resistance. Nothing here is cairned or named.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS EXPLICIT AND IT HAS A STATED CONSEQUENCE: misidentifying the correct gully near the col leads to an exposed low-fifth-class DEAD END. If the ground you are on has stopped offering an easy option and is committing you to fifth-class moves, reverse and pick a different line — this route never needs them.

THE CRUX IS SHORT AND IT IS AT THE TOP: the step gaining the SUMMIT RIDGE is loose and exposed Class 2-3 and is the hardest ground on the route. After it, an easy traverse of about 100 ft to the WEST — to your right — reaches the top. If you gain a ridge and the summit is to your left, you are on the wrong section of crest.

GOING BACK DOWN, USE A DIFFERENT LINE THAN YOU CAME UP FOR ONE STRETCH ONLY: below the benches, the vegetated slopes beside the talus gullies are the better descent, and the loose climber's-left skyline gully should be avoided.
hazards: Misidentifying the gully near the col, which leads to an exposed low-fifth-class dead end
Loose, sandy rock flanking the col and loose talus on the upper mountain
Cornices and early-season snow at the Fortress-Chiwawa col
An unbridged ford of the Chiwawa headwater, and fading braided tread that becomes a bushwhack if you drift into timber
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat, so Trinity is currently unreachable by vehicle

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek variant to the col west of the summit
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Sep, as for the main line
approach_variants.notes:
A less-travelled alternative starts at the Phelps Creek Trailhead rather than Trinity. It bushwhacks to about 5,500 ft and follows a gully to the right of Point 5971 up to the col WEST of the summit, then takes easy Class 2 ground along the west ridge to the top.

This is the shorter line on paper and the rougher one on the ground: there is no tread on the bushwhack and no camp equivalent to the Chiwawa Basin benches. It is recorded here because it exists and is genuinely used, not because it is recommended over the Trinity approach.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS VARIANT'S BASE IS A DIFFERENT COL FROM THE MAIN ROUTE'S, AND CONFUSING THE TWO PUTS YOU ON THE WRONG SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN. The standard line goes to the FORTRESS-CHIWAWA col, which is SOUTH-WEST of the summit and is a notch in Fortress's east ridge. This variant goes to the col WEST of the summit, gained from Phelps Creek by a gully to the RIGHT of Point 5971.

THE TEST IS WHAT LIES ABOVE THE COL YOU REACH. From this one, the WEST RIDGE runs to the summit on easy Class 2 ground — a walk, essentially. From the Fortress-Chiwawa col you face slabs, gullies and talus on the south-west FACE with a loose Class 2-3 step at the top. If you have reached a col and the way on is a broad easy crest, you are on this variant. If it is a face with no obvious line, you are on the standard one.

THE APPROACH MARKER IS A NUMBERED POINT AND THAT IS ALL THERE IS: the gully is to the RIGHT of Point 5971. Nothing else about the bushwhack below it is published, which is why this is the second variant and not the first. Carry a track.
hazards: An unmaintained bushwhack with no tread from about 5,500 ft and no published landmarks below the gully
No established camp on this side, so it commits you to a long day
Early-season snow in the gully and at the col
Loose rock on the west ridge, as everywhere on this peak

approach_variants.name: Trinity and the Chiwawa River Trail to the Chiwawa-Fortress col
approach_variants.season: Jun-Oct. Crampons and an axe are commonly used on the snow slopes crossing to the col even in late summer
approach_variants.notes:
From Trinity Trailhead near 2,800 ft at the end of FR-6200, follow the Buck Creek and Chiwawa River trails up-valley beneath Red Mountain to about 6,580 ft, then leave the trail and traverse diagonally up toward Chiwawa Mountain's east ridge, descending to the roughly 7,200 ft col between Chiwawa and Fortress. Some parties go over Chiwawa's summit first instead. Others approach by way of the Red Mountain Trail and Chiwawa Basin, fording the Chiwawa River — the same basin the Chiwawa Mountain route uses, which puts you on the col from below rather than from along the ridge.

The col is a common high camp and this route is very often combined with Chiwawa Mountain from it, which is the practical reason to camp there rather than lower.

Rock quality is notably BETTER on the East Ridge itself than in the gully that gains it or on Fortress's south-west face — the opposite of what most parties expect.

FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat, adding roughly seven miles of road-walking each way.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL IS THE CAMP AND THE GULLY IS THE ROUTE, AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME PLACE. From the roughly 7,200 ft Chiwawa-Fortress col, the East Ridge is gained by a LOOSE CLASS 3-4 GULLY. Standing on the col is not standing at the base; you still have a gully to find and climb before the ridge starts.

THE ROCK ITSELF IS THE CONFIRMATION, AND IT WORKS BACKWARDS FROM WHAT YOU WOULD GUESS: the gully is the loose ground and the ridge above it is the SOLID ground. So the test that you have topped out of the correct gully onto the correct crest is that the rock gets BETTER. If you have gained a crest and it is still rubble, you are on a subsidiary rib rather than the East Ridge.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER ROUTE ON THIS MOUNTAIN: the south-west face is reached from an entirely different valley — Buck Creek Trail and Pass No Pass at about 6,400 ft — and never comes near this col. If your approach involved a way-trail and a pass rather than a cross-country traverse off the Chiwawa River Trail, you are on the other side of the peak.

THE FINISH IS ONE MOVE AND IT IS UNPROTECTED IN PRACTICE: an exposed fourth-class step just below the summit, normally climbed unroped. That step is the route's crux and its arrival marker — reaching it means the ridge is behind you.

COMING BACK DOWN, THE HEAD OF THE GULLY IS THE THING TO FIND, and it is easier to walk past from above than from below. Follow the crest back until the ground drops away toward the col, and descend carefully; the gully is the loosest part of the day in both directions.

IF YOU CONTINUE TO CHIWAWA MOUNTAIN from the col — which many parties do — note that its route works up the SOUTH-WEST side on slabs and talus from that same col, so the two climbs share a base and diverge immediately.
hazards: Loose rock in the gully gaining the East Ridge from the col — the worst ground on the route, and reversed on the way down
An exposed, normally unroped fourth-class step on the final summit pitch
Cold thigh- to knee-deep fords of the Chiwawa River drainage on the Chiwawa Basin approach
Steep firm snow crossing to the col, wanting crampons and an axe even late in the season
About seven extra miles of road-walking each way while FR-6200 is closed beyond Atkinson Flat

approach_variants.name: Buck Creek Trail #1513 and the Pass No Pass way-trail
approach_variants.season: Jun-Oct, best Jul-Sep once the south-west face has melted out; an axe and sometimes crampons for early-season snow on the approach slopes below the pass
approach_variants.notes:
From Trinity Trailhead at 2,800 ft, follow Buck Creek Trail #1513 roughly nine to nine and a half miles, climbing through forest and an old avalanche debris field near 4,500 ft.

The turn is the thing to watch for and it is NOT MARKED: an unmarked junction with the Pass No Pass way-trail bears RIGHT at about 5,800 ft. Follow the way-trail to Pass No Pass near 6,400 ft and the alpine camping benches beyond it, from which the face and the south ridge come into view.

Since 2026 storm damage has closed FR-6200 to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat Campground around mile 16, adding roughly seven miles of road-walking each way before you even reach the trailhead.

From a high camp in the Pass No Pass basin, parties report about three and a half to four hours up and two and a half to three back.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE PASS IS WHERE THE MOUNTAIN BECOMES VISIBLE, AND THAT IS THE ARRIVAL TEST: from Pass No Pass and the benches beyond it, Fortress's SOUTH-WEST FACE AND SOUTH RIDGE COME INTO VIEW. Below the pass you cannot see the peak at all. If you are still walking with no mountain in front of you, you have not crossed it.

THE CLIMBING STARTS AT A CHANGE OF SURFACE, NOT AT A FEATURE. From the basin below the pass, green slopes and scree steepen into Class 2-3 talus and slab. There is no step, no toe and no notch to arrive at — grass gives way to rock and that is the base.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE MOST USEFUL SENTENCE ON THIS ROUTE: THE DIRECT GULLY UP THE FACE IS THE LOOSEST GROUND ON THE MOUNTAIN. If you are in a defined gully with rubble moving under every step, you are on the line to avoid, not the line to take. Angle RIGHT onto slabbier rock, or follow the south ridge crest instead. A party in 2015 found and cairned an alternate Class 3 line over more solid blocky terrain to skier's right of the gully, and later parties have followed it — so cairns on solid blocky ground here are a good sign, which is the reverse of the situation in the gully.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER SIDE OF THIS PEAK: the East Ridge is reached from the Chiwawa-Fortress col at about 7,200 ft, approached cross-country off the Chiwawa River Trail, and it starts with a loose Class 3-4 gully onto a crest of notably better rock. Nothing on that route involves a way-trail or a named pass. If you walked over a pass to get here, you are on the south-west side.

THE SUMMIT BLOCK IS TALUS. There is no technical finish on this route; if you are looking at a fourth-class step you have wandered onto the east side's ground.
hazards: The direct south-west gully is the loosest ground on the mountain and is directly above anyone below
Steep snow on the approach slopes below Pass No Pass into early summer, needing self-arrest skills
An unmarked way-trail junction at about 5,800 ft that is easy to walk past on a nine-mile approach
Creek crossings and brushy, indistinct trail lower down
Roughly seven extra miles of road-walking each way while FR-6200 is closed beyond Atkinson Flat

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin to the west side of the peak
approach_variants.season: Aug-Sep. This is explicitly a late-season line — it wants the snow gone and the rock dry
approach_variants.notes:
The lower approach is shared with the peak's north-side routes: Phelps Creek Trailhead at about 3,500 ft off FR-6211, Phelps Creek Trail #1511 to the Leroy Creek ford at roughly 3.5 miles, then the unmaintained Leroy Creek high route steeply up into Leroy Basin around 6,100-6,200 ft, where the established camps are. That climbers' trail gains about 1,200 ft per mile — it is short and steep and hot under an overnight pack.

Where this route parts company with its neighbours is at the basin: instead of heading for the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col or the Icy Lake notch, it continues onto the peak's WEST side to reach the couloir system near the standard West / South Slopes ground.

The climb is short — roughly 450 m of mostly slabby Class 3 with two brief Class 4 steps — and it pairs naturally with a descent of the South Shoulder to make a loop back into Leroy Basin rather than a there-and-back.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE GULLY IS FOUND BY COUNTING, AND THE THING YOU COUNT FROM IS THE NORTH TOWER. From the west side of the mountain the route is THE SECOND GULLY TO THE RIGHT OF THE NORTH TOWER. Not the first, not the third. That is the entire identification, and it works in poor light because a tower is a silhouette rather than a texture.

THE POSITIVE TEST ONCE YOU ARE IN IT: the line takes the SHALLOW RIGHT FORK up slabby Class 3 rock on clean stone. Shallow, right, slabby, clean. A gully that stays a single deep cleft with no fork, or one whose rock is rubble rather than slab, is the wrong count.

THE SECOND CONFIRMATION IS A SIDEWAYS MOVE: after the first slabs the route steps RIGHT into ANOTHER couloir over a brief Class 4 step, then continues on sustained slabby Class 3 to the ridge crest. So the correct sequence is fork right, then move right again. If your gully runs straight to the crest with no lateral move and no short hard step, you are not on this line.

WHAT THE TOP OF THE ROUTE IS NOT: gaining the ridge crest is not the summit. From the crest the route TRAVERSES SOUTH toward the main summit, passing around towers on the WEST — the right — side, with occasional brief Class 4 moves. If you top out and start going north, you are walking away from the peak.

THE DISCRIMINATORS AGAINST THIS PEAK'S OTHER ROUTES, all three of which start from the same basin: the North Face route crosses the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col and then DESCENDS four hundred feet on the far side before it reaches anything; the ice-fall route goes through a notch at about 7,200 ft onto the Entiat Glacier. Both of those take you AWAY from the west side. If you have crossed a col or gone through a notch, you have left this route — it never leaves the peak's own west flank.

CARRY THE MEANS TO PROTECT ONE MOVE, OR NOTHING. Most parties solo this; the Class 4 steps are brief and unprotected in practice, and there is nothing on the route that a rope helps with except those.
hazards: Loose rock among the summit-ridge towers on the traverse south
Brief exposed Class 4 moves that most parties climb without protection
Miscounting the gullies from the North Tower, which puts you on unrecorded ground on the same face
A steep unmaintained climbers' trail into Leroy Basin gaining roughly 1,200 ft per mile
A late-season route on an east-side peak, so afternoon thunderstorms and smoke are the normal conditions

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin over Leroy and Freezer passes to the Ice Lakes basin
approach_variants.season: Aug is the reliable month. Early-to-mid July can still hold snow and high water on the Freezer Pass traverse and at the washed-out stream bed; late September adds larch colour and takes away daylight
approach_variants.notes:
From the Phelps Creek Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, Phelps Creek Trail #1511 climbs the east side of the valley at roughly 275 ft per mile, crossing into the wilderness at 2.6 miles and reaching the Leroy Creek ford at about 3.5. Immediately across the ford the unmaintained Leroy Creek high route branches steeply north-east and climbs 1.9 miles into Leroy Basin at about 5,400 ft, where the camps are. That half is hot and exposed under a pack.

From camp pick up the Carne Mountain high trail — an old sheepherder track — south-east; it gives up a little height to cross the south fork of Leroy Creek before climbing to Leroy Pass at 6,850 ft. Cairns mark the way but several paths braid apart in the basin: stay on the LOWER and better-trodden line where they diverge.

Continue east on faint footpaths through heather, then talus and scree, gaining about 750 ft over roughly a mile to Freezer Pass at 7,600 ft. There is no maintained tread here and the boot paths come and go, so TRACK YOUR OWN LINE FOR THE RETURN.

Drop north-east off the pass into the Ice Lakes basin, losing about 1,000 ft past the north end of Upper Ice Lake and down the dry stream bed to the west shore of Lower Ice Lake. Both lakes are reliable water.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
