THE BASE IS AN OPEN BASIN FLOOR BETWEEN TWO SUMMITS AND THAT IS WHY IT IS FINDABLE IN CLOUD — you are not looking for a feature on a face, you are walking into a gap between the two Buttes at about 6,800 ft. The traverse eases into it. If the ground is still side-hilling and everything moves under your feet, you have not arrived.

GETTING THERE, THE ONE PLACE PEOPLE GET HURT: from Lower Ice Lake the old Ice Lakes Trail fades and you SIDEHILL EAST AT ABOUT 6,600 FT on slippery scrub and loose rock with no tread. Keep the party STRUNG OUT IN A LINE rather than stacked one above another — almost everything here moves. About a third of a mile brings the lip of a WASHED-OUT GULLY. Downclimb the loose clay and scree into it and climb the far side back to ABOUT THE SAME ELEVATION.

THAT ELEVATION RULE IS THE NEGATIVE MARKER AND IT HAS A STATED CONSEQUENCE: DROPPING TOO LOW IN THE WASHOUT LEAVES YOU CLIFFED OUT. Cross at 6,600, not below it. This is also the last reliable water before the summit, so fill there.

THE CLIMBING STARTS AT A RAMP: from the basin floor, a SCREE-AND-TALUS RAMP of about 400 ft gains the crest of the south-west ridge. Ramp first, ridge second. If you are on the crest without having walked up 400 ft of scree, you got onto the ridge somewhere else.

THE SIDE RULE ON THE RIDGE, AND IT IS ABSOLUTE: broken crags and short cliff bands repeatedly force the route OFF the crest onto ledges on the SOUTH side. THE NORTH SIDE OF THE RIDGE IS CLIFFY AND SHOULD NOT BE ENTERED. If you have been pushed off the crest and the ground below you drops away in a way that feels wrong, check which side you stepped onto before you commit.

THE CRUX HAS AN ELEVATION: around 7,700 ft a spire forces a short chossy chute, a traverse on down-sloping rock, and a Class 3 dike. Some parties call it low Class 4. That is the hardest ground and it is a single passage, not a section.

CAIRNS HERE BLEND INTO THE ROCK. On the way up that costs time; on the way down it costs a great deal more, because from the summit block you have to find the crest again at about 8,100 ft. Pick the line up deliberately rather than drifting down the first ledge system that goes.
hazards: A washed-out gully crossing at 6,600 ft where dropping too low cliffs you out
Sustained loose rock and talus on the ridge and the scree ramp, with real rockfall risk onto anyone below
The north side of the south-west ridge is cliffy and must not be entered when the crags force you off the crest
No reliable water beyond the washout crossing — carry four to five litres in summer heat
Cairns that blend into the surrounding rock across the Ice Lakes traverse and on the descent from the summit block

approach_variants.name: Boulder Pass and the sheepherder's traverse to the col west of Clark Mountain, then the upper Richardson Glacier
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, with August the most reliable. The Richardson has been reported thinning and breaking up in recent years, so a late-season party should expect it to be less straightforward than older accounts describe
approach_variants.notes:
From the White River Trailhead near 2,300 ft at the end of FR-6400, White River Trail #1507 runs almost level upstream through old growth for about four miles. The junction with Boulder Creek Trail #1562 sits roughly a quarter mile PAST the bridge over Boulder Creek — if you have crossed the creek and seen no sign, keep walking.

Turn onto #1562 and climb gently through forest to the established camp at the creek crossing near 3,700 ft; whether that is a step-across or a genuine ford depends on the year. Above camp the trail switchbacks and climbs roughly 2,500-2,700 ft over about three miles into the open basin below Boulder Pass. Snow lingers in that basin well into summer, and the pass is the last of the maintained, easy-to-follow trail.

Above Boulder Pass the route becomes an unmaintained sheepherder's path that sidehills EAST across a series of cirques, losing roughly 1,000 ft as it traverses below Clark Mountain's south spur before regaining height near a 7,200 ft spur. That traverse is the route-finding crux of the approach: brushy, exposed to sidehill slips, and easy to lose in poor visibility or under snow.

This row also carries a set of waypoints describing a different line — over the pass, down to a ford of the Napeequa near 4,700 ft, and up to a high basin at 7,000 ft under the east face. Both are real ways to this mountain; see _DEFECTS.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING IS A GLACIER, AND THE THING THAT GETS YOU TO IT IS A COL THAT BELONGS TO THE NEXT PEAK. From the 7,200 ft spur, make a RISING traverse across broad benches — often snow-covered well into summer — and easy Class 2 ledges to the roughly 7,600 ft COL WEST OF CLARK MOUNTAIN. You are navigating to a gap beside a different summit, which is what makes it findable: Clark is the big thing on your left.

FROM THAT COL, THE ROUTE IS ONE RISING TRAVERSE ACROSS THE UPPER RICHARDSON GLACIER TO LUAHNA'S EAST RIDGE. Rope up at the col. The glacier crossing is the route; the ridge above it is a scramble west to the summit.

THE CRITICAL NEGATIVE MARKER IS ABOUT WHICH GLACIER YOU ARE ON, and this peak's own record has already been wrong about it once: THE PILZ AND BUTTERFLY GLACIERS ARE ON LUAHNA'S NORTH SLOPE AND BELONG TO A SEPARATE ROUTE APPROACHED FROM THE NAPEEQUA SIDE. This route uses the RICHARDSON, which lies to the SOUTH-EAST of the summit. If the glacier you have stepped onto is north of the peak, you are on the other mountain's business entirely.

THE SECOND NEGATIVE MARKER IS SIMPLER: if you never touched a glacier at all, you are on the south-west slopes and south-east ridge line, which is the other route on this peak and is deliberately glacier-free. Both finish on the same summit and neither is a variation of the other.

COMING DOWN, THE ONE PIECE OF TECHNICAL GROUND IS BELOW THE EAST RIDGE: a short, steep step reported as low Class 4 and sometimes verglassed in an adjacent gully. Strong parties downclimb it; a single 20-30 m rappel off a horn or block is common practice when it is wet or icy. There is no fixed anchor — carry webbing.

DO NOT TAKE THE THUNDER CREEK EXIT ON THE STRENGTH OF THE MAP. Dropping south into Thunder Creek looks shorter and is reported slower and rougher, with heavy blowdown, avalanche debris and a boot path that disappears near the creek crossing. Reversing the ascent line over Boulder Pass is the reliable way out.
hazards: Crevasses and moats on an upper Richardson Glacier that recent parties report thinning and breaking up
The sheepherder's traverse across the cirques — brushy, exposed to sidehill slips, and easy to lose in cloud or snow
A short low Class 4 step below the east ridge that can carry verglas and has no fixed anchor
Loose scree and rotten rock just below the summit block
A Thunder Creek exit that reads shorter on the map and is documented as slower, brushier and harder to follow

approach_variants.name: Boulder Basin high camp and the sheepherder's trail through four cirques
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep. A September ascent works but expect cold and the possibility of early snow on the traverse and the summit ledges
approach_variants.notes:
From the White River Trailhead near 2,300 ft, White River Trail #1507 and then Boulder Creek Trail #1562 lead to a ford and camp around 3,700 ft, and on up into Boulder Basin. High camp is a grassy knoll overlooking the basin at about 5,800 ft.

From camp the route traverses a saddle into the White River drainage and then follows the old sheepherder's path across a chain of cirques. The path is fairly well defined but the FIRST cirque is where parties lose it and regain it repeatedly; the second, Clark Basin, is less brushy, more open and park-like with clear tread; the third, Luahna Basin, has good tread and is where parties describe camping as heaven on earth.

There is a great deal of up-and-down and side-hilling on this traverse — the elevation figure on file for this row is far larger than for the peak's other route, which is what all that sidehill costs.

This line is deliberately glacier-free, which is its whole reason to exist beside the other route on the peak.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU FIND THE BASE OF THIS ROUTE BY COUNTING BASINS, AND THE ANSWER IS FOUR. From the Boulder Basin camp the sheepherder's path crosses cirques in order: BOULDER, then CLARK, then LUAHNA, and the peak's base sits above the FOURTH — Chalangin Basin. Nothing about the ground tells you which cirque you are in, but the character does: the first is where the path keeps disappearing, the second is open and park-like, the third has good tread. Count them.

THE INTERMEDIATE MARKER IS A NUMBER ON THE RIDGE: make a rising traverse across Luahna Basin toward the roughly 7,500 ft RIDGE POINT, then follow a faint trail across scree and talus ABOVE the fourth cirque to the peak's base. Above Chalangin Basin, not in it.

THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE BASE IS THE GRADE, AND IT IS EASIER THAN YOU EXPECT: the scramble begins on EASY CLASS 2 LEDGES on the SOUTH FACE, leading up to the right-hand skyline ridge. Class 2 ledges, south-facing, and a ridge on your right at the top of them. If your first ground is steep, or if you are on a glacier, or if the ledges lead left, you are not on it.

THE CONFIRMATION COMES HIGH AND IT IS ON THE WRONG SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN: just beneath the summit the route crosses an EXPOSED CLASS 3+ TRAVERSE ON THE NORTH SIDE before the final Class 3 scramble straight up. So the sequence is south-face ledges, gain the ridge, cross to the NORTH beneath the summit, then straight up. A route that never leaves the sunny side has not reached the summit block.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER AGAINST THE PEAK'S OTHER ROUTE: the east slopes line crosses the upper RICHARDSON GLACIER from a col west of Clark Mountain and needs glacier gear. This route touches no glacier at all. If you are roping up for crevasses, you are on the other one, and it is a different day.

A NOTE ON WHAT THE GUIDEBOOK SAYS VERSUS WHAT PARTIES FIND: this is described as a second-class line, and most parties meet a short Class 3 or better traverse or step to bypass a gap in the ridge below the true summit. Expect it rather than treat it as evidence you are off route.
hazards: An exposed Class 3+ traverse on the NORTH side just beneath the summit, crossed with nothing to protect it
A long sidehilling traverse across four cirques with heavy elevation loss and regain, and a path that vanishes in the first one
Loose scree and rotten rock below the summit block
Lingering snow on the traverse and ledges early in the season
Remoteness measured in a day's walk from any road, with no cell coverage

approach_variants.name: Little Giant Trail #1518 over the pass and down into the Napeequa
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable. The Chiwawa ford at the very start of this trail is waist-deep and swift in early season and is only reliably safe in late-summer and autumn low water
approach_variants.notes:
The Little Giant Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft roughly mile 19 of Chiwawa River Road, three miles down-valley of Trinity. The trail begins with an UNBRIDGED FORD OF THE CHIWAWA RIVER, right at the start — there is no way around it and it is the gate on the whole approach.

Trail #1518 then climbs steeply and badly-eroded to Little Giant Pass at 6,463 ft, with a small spring a few hundred feet below the pass at about 6,250 ft that is the last dependable water before the high basins. Maintained tread effectively ends at the pass.

From the pass the route drops toward the Louis Creek and Napeequa basin, then follows a climbers' path upstream to the end of tread at the creek draining Berge's south-west side. A steep, intermittent boot track climbs through timber to treeline and opens into the south-west basin. A narrow notch at about 7,840 ft in the ridge crest links the Louis Creek basin to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face, and gaining it is exposed scrambling.

All options to this peak are 15-plus miles round trip and are multi-day trips.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A BROAD SADDLE ON THE SOUTH SIDE AT ABOUT 7,650 FT, AND THE WAY YOU GET TO IT IS A SNOW FINGER RATHER THAN A SLOPE. Near a snowfield around 7,000 ft the line uses a SNOW FINGER AND ITS MOAT, plus steep heather, to reach that saddle below the final summit block. Looking for a walkable slope will not find it; looking for the place where snow runs up into a narrowing tongue against rock will.

THE SADDLE IS WHERE THE ROUTE LEAVES THE BASIN. Below it you are traversing basins; above it you are climbing rock bands and steep heather toward the summit ridge. If you are still contouring, you are below it.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING ON THIS PEAK AND IT IS ABOUT ASPECT: BERGE'S NORTH AND WEST FACES ARE CLIFFY. Parties must stay on the SOUTH-WEST side. Do not try to go straight up from High Pass — the direct line from the north does not go. If the ground above you is steepening into walls rather than rock bands and heather, you are on the wrong side of the mountain.

THE ROUTE-FINDING RULE LOWER DOWN IS A DESCENDING TRAVERSE, WHICH FEELS WRONG AND IS RIGHT: near 5,400 ft the described line drops across into meadows, and it is from those meadows that several scrambling lines reach the top. Losing height on an approach to a summit is expected here.

THE LAST OBSTACLE HAS AN ELEVATION AND A CHARACTER: an exposed gully near 7,800 ft with SLANTED SLABS and real exposure near its top. Holds and ledges are solid and the passage is straightforward, and a slip there would be consequential — helmet.

THE SUMMIT IS NOT ONE POINT. The TRUE, NORTH summit needs a short FOURTH-CLASS step, harder than the third-class south summit. Standing on the easier top is not standing on the mountain.
hazards: An unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River at the very start of Little Giant Trail, waist-deep and swift outside late-season low water
Berge's north and west faces are cliffy and the direct line from High Pass does not go
A steep, badly eroded trail to Little Giant Pass and no maintained tread beyond it
An exposed gully of slanted slabs near 7,800 ft where a slip has serious consequences
A short fourth-class step to the true north summit, harder than the rest of the route

approach_variants.name: Trinity and Buck Creek, or the High Pass high route from Buck Creek Pass
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable
approach_variants.notes:
Two other ways reach the same mountain from the Trinity side.

The EAST approach: from Trinity, follow Chiwawa River Trail #1550 about two miles to the Buck Creek Trail #1513 junction, then Buck Creek Trail roughly four to five miles into the basin Berge shares with Mount Cleator and Buck Mountain on its east side.

The NORTH approach: continue past the Buck Creek junction to Buck Creek Pass, then take the climbers' path over High Pass and contour SOUTH under Berge's north side near Point 7839. This is the longest by mileage and has the least off-trail travel, which is the trade it offers.

Both involve unbridged or damaged creek crossings and both are multi-day. FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which affects the drive to Trinity.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HIGH PASS APPROACH DELIVERS YOU TO THE WRONG SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN ON PURPOSE, AND THE RULE IS THAT YOU MUST KEEP GOING AROUND. Contouring south under Berge's north side puts a cliffy face above you. THE CLIMB IS ON THE SOUTH-WEST SIDE. Carry on around until the ground above you is rock bands and steep heather rather than wall, and only then start up.

THE ARRIVAL IS THE SAME PLACE FOR EVERY APPROACH TO THIS PEAK: the broad SADDLE ON BERGE'S SOUTH SIDE AT ABOUT 7,650 FT, where the south-west slopes route leaves the basin. Whichever valley you came up, that saddle is what you are walking to.

THE APPROACH-SPECIFIC MARKER ON THE HIGH PASS LINE is a numbered point rather than a shape: you contour beneath Point 7839. If you are still north of it you have not gone far enough around.

THE 7,840 FT NOTCH IS THE LINK BETWEEN THE TWO SIDES and it is worth knowing exists whichever way you came: a narrow notch in the ridge crest connects the Louis Creek basin on the Napeequa side to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face. Gaining it is exposed scrambling, and it is the reason the two approaches meet at all.

AND THE SAME SUMMIT WARNING APPLIES: the true summit is the NORTH one and it takes a short fourth-class step. The south summit is third class and is not the top.
hazards: Berge's north face is cliffy — the direct line from High Pass does not go, and this approach puts you underneath it
Unbridged or damaged creek crossings on both the Buck Creek and Napeequa approaches
Brush and blowdown on unmaintained climbers' paths above the end of tread
An exposed 7,840 ft notch linking the two sides of the ridge
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat, affecting the drive to Trinity

approach_variants.name: Buck Creek Trail, Mount Cleator's east ridge and the alder tunnel to the twin gendarmes
approach_variants.season: Summer into autumn; carry an ice axe before August for lingering snow on the approach traverse
approach_variants.notes:
From the Trinity / Buck Creek Trailhead, hike roughly six miles of Buck Creek Trail through an old burn recovering in fireweed, then drop through a meadow and ford Buck Creek — an easy crossing in normal summer flow.

Across the creek, climb to the crest of MOUNT CLEATOR'S east ridge through logged and burned forest with a great deal of downed timber. The forest opens considerably above about 4,800 ft, and around 5,500 ft a faint trail appears and contours LEFT.

That faint path leads to an ALDER TUNNEL at the base of some cliffs. Breaking out of it, traverse slippery heather and blueberry slopes across a basin beneath a waterfall, then climb steep goat trails to a grassy knoll beside a talus field.

The route is nearly 2,000 vertical feet of generally low-angle, low- to mid-fifth granite, broken by a distinct notch and a burly 5.8 chimney crux, then towers and gendarmes to the summit. Rock is consistently solid enough for fast simul-climbing except at the crux — which is what makes this the peak's one technical line.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO GENDARMES MARK THE START OF THE RIDGE, AND THE ROUTE GOES UP THE GULLY TO THEIR RIGHT — NOT BETWEEN THEM AND NOT TO THEIR LEFT. That is the whole identification, and it is a countable one: TWO towers side by side, and you take the weakness on the RIGHT-hand side of the pair.

WHAT THE GULLY LOOKS LIKE, SO YOU DO NOT REJECT IT: it is mangy. Loose, easy to mid-fifth-class scrambling, with the upper section the loosest — parties have gone up it in running shoes with full overnight packs. It is not attractive and it is correct. A clean-looking line beside it is not the route.

WHERE THE GULLY DELIVERS YOU, AND THIS IS WHERE THE CLIMBING PROPER STARTS: the NOTCH beside the twin gendarmes. Rope up there, not at the base of the gully.

THE APPROACH MARKER IMMEDIATELY BELOW IS A GRASSY KNOLL NEXT TO A TALUS FIELD, reached by steep goat trails out of the heather-and-blueberry basin under a waterfall. Grass, then talus, then two towers. If you are still in alder or on heather, you are below it.

THE ONE THING THAT WILL COST YOU THE MOST TIME LOWER DOWN is the contour at about 5,500 ft. The faint trail goes LEFT into an alder tunnel at the base of cliffs; the tunnel is the way through, not an obstacle to avoid. A party that stays on the ridge crest above it ends up cliffed against the same band the tunnel undercuts.

THE DESCENT DECISION IS MADE BEFORE YOU START: the recommended way back reverses the approach over the Berge-Cleator saddle, and the KEY IS A LEDGE TRAVERSE ABOVE THE LOWER SLABS which avoids losing and regaining height. Below that it is brushy, wet alder and steep heather back to the boot path. The alternative drops west via the High Pass trail, adds distance, and is really only worth it if you are also climbing Buck Mountain.
hazards: Extensive loose rock along the ridge, including trundle-prone blocks at the 5.8 chimney crux
A loose mid-fifth-class approach gully climbed by most parties unroped with overnight packs
Weather closing in fast on the exposed upper ridge, where the towers all look alike in poor visibility
A wet, brushy, muddy descent traverse that is materially worse after rain
Heavy downed timber in the burn on Cleator's east ridge, and an alder tunnel that has to be found rather than avoided

approach_variants.name: North Fork Entiat Trail #1437 to the Pyramid Mountain junction, then the west-side basin
approach_variants.season: Late May-Sep. In late May and June this is effectively a snow climb — the gully to the saddle holds 40-50 degree snow and wants an axe and crampons. By August it dries into loose Class 3 talus
approach_variants.notes:
From the end of FR-5606 at the North Fork Entiat Trailhead near 3,940 ft, take North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437. The lower trail is OUTSIDE the wilderness, so mountain bikes are legal on the first several miles and many parties use one on a 20-mile round trip.

The first six miles follow the river on a gentle forested grade, straight through old burn. The river is the last reliable water — everything above is dry — so fill before leaving the valley. Expect to work over, under and around blowdown, and to lose the tread briefly among downed timber; Grouse Creek is crossed on a log inside one of the worst of those stretches.

A signed spur to Fern Lake splits off at about mile 6.1 — stay on #1437. Around mile 7 near 5,800 ft the trail bends sharply EAST and switchbacks about half a mile to its end at the Pyramid Mountain Trail #1433 junction near 6,600 ft. That junction is a useful timing landmark: the summit is roughly a mile from it.

Leave the trail there and head east through sparse forest and then talus toward the peak's west and south-west flank. A camp flat sits around 7,100 ft in the open basin.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A GULLY THAT LEADS TO A GAP BETWEEN TWO SUMMITS, AND THE GAP IS WHAT YOU NAVIGATE TO — NOT THE PEAK. From the basin camp, contour onto the peak's WESTERN slopes and work SOUTH below the summit ridge across steep talus and scree until you are underneath the broad gully leading to the NOTCH BETWEEN THE NORTH AND MIDDLE SUMMITS, at about 8,300 ft. Every party uses that same notch whichever flank they approached from, so it is the one landmark this mountain has.

THE GULLY IS BROAD, NOT A CLEFT, AND IT FACES NORTH-WEST. Early season it is moderately steep snow up to about 40 degrees; later it is loose Class 2 talus and scree the whole way. If the feature above you is a narrow slot, or if it is not the widest weakness on that stretch of face, you are under the wrong one.

THE CONFIRMATION IS WHAT HAPPENS AT THE TOP OF IT: you arrive on a SADDLE with summits on BOTH sides of you. From there the ground is a ridge scramble along or just east of the crest. If you top out of a gully onto a single continuous slope rather than a gap, you are not there.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS ABOUT THE SUMMIT AND IT DECIDES WHETHER YOUR DAY IS OVER: the ridge from the saddle leads to the MIDDLE summit, which is non-technical and where most scramblers stop. The TRUE summit is the slightly higher SOUTH one, and reaching it takes a SHORT EXPOSED STEP — described historically as a vertical chimney onto a foot-wide summit ridge, unrated and treated by every account as the crux. If you have walked to a top without meeting a hard move, you are on the middle summit.

THE THING THAT SENDS PARTIES HERE FROM THE NORTH SIDE, worth knowing so you recognise it if you meet them: when the north ridge holds snow and verglas, parties abandon it and drop onto the east and south-east slopes below the summit ridge to finish — this route's ground. That is a documented retreat, not an error.

STOW CRAMPONS AT THE TOP OF THE GULLY if the rock above is dry. The exposure on the ridge is real and the moves near the top run Class 3 and arguably Class 4.
hazards: A gully that is loose top to bottom in summer and 40-50 degree snow through June, with the whole party in the fall line
An exposed, sometimes-corniced summit ridge traverse of roughly 500 ft with genuine consequence
A short unrated technical step between the middle summit and the true south summit that many parties decline
Constant loose rock on the traverse below the summit ridge, so parties must not stack up
A dry, long approach through burn with heavy blowdown, and no water above the valley

approach_variants.name: North Fork Entiat to the Pyramid Mountain junction, then the basin between Saska and Emerald
approach_variants.season: Mid-Jul-Sep for snow-free scrambling; late May and June need an axe and crampons for neve in the summit gullies. October is popular for larch colour and brings short days
approach_variants.notes:
From the North Fork Entiat River Trailhead near 3,940 ft at the end of FR-5606, take Trail #1437 upstream on a gentle grade — only about 1,300 ft of gain over six miles. The lower miles run through old burn and blowdown, so plan on working over and around deadfall rather than walking clean tread. Grouse Creek has been crossed on a logjam roughly 100 ft upstream of the trail crossing, or on a deteriorating footbridge, depending on the year.

Bear right at the Fern Lake fork and stay on #1437. Around mile 7 the trail swings sharply east and switchbacks half a mile to its end at the Pyramid Mountain Trail junction. In early season the tread gets hard to follow once snow patches start above roughly 4,800 ft.

Leave the maintained trail at the junction and head west; the timber opens into a clearing within about a quarter mile. FILL AND TREAT WATER THERE — the valley bottom is the last easy water and there is little of it above.

From the clearing the travel is cross-country: angle west then south-west, contouring below Cardinal Peak's west side toward the basin system south of Emerald. Expect to GIVE BACK 200-300 ft to skirt cliff bands before regaining the open basin floor around 6,900 ft. A camp flat sits near 7,000-7,100 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START OF THE CLIMBING IS THE UPPER BASIN WEDGED BETWEEN SASKA AND EMERALD, AND THE THING THAT LEADS YOU INTO IT IS RUNNING WATER. From the 6,900 ft basin, cross a shoulder near 7,100 ft and climb a gully system into that upper basin. THE SLABBY WATERCOURSE DRAINING IT GIVES THE MOST CONTINUOUS LINE and holds snow well into early summer — so in cloud, follow the drainage uphill rather than picking a gully by eye.

THE ARRIVAL IS A BENCH AT ABOUT 7,800 FT beneath the south-east side of the summit ridge. From there several scramble lines look much alike and NONE IS OBVIOUSLY BETTER THAN THE REST. That is the honest state of this route and it is why the rule below is a direction rather than a description.

THE RULE IS: WORK UP AND TO CLIMBERS' RIGHT TO STAY ON THE STANDARD LINE. Right, from the bench. If you have drifted left you are on one of the variations that this face is full of, and they do not all go.

WHAT THE CORRECT GULLY DOES AT ITS TOP, which is the confirmation: it TOPS OUT AT A NOTCH IN THE SUMMIT RIDGE, and from that notch it is only a SHORT Class 2-3 scramble to the top — one described account calls it a very short Class 3 scramble near the top. So the test is proportion: if you have topped out of a gully and there is a great deal of climbing still above you, you are in the wrong gully.

THE SUMMIT IS TWO POINTS ABOUT 100 FT APART and the NORTH one is the true, marginally higher top. The south point is a noticeably steeper inclined slab and a slip off it runs down the EAST FACE. The whole summit area is small and drops away within a few paces in most directions, and several nearby lower rock points can be mistaken for the summit — so the exposure, not the difficulty, is what deserves attention at the top.

WHAT THIS ROUTE IS NOT: it is not a ridge climb despite the name. The name describes the ridge and notch it gains relative to Cardinal Peak, which sits just to the south-east. The climbing is a gully and a short scramble.
hazards: Loose rock and choss in the summit gullies, with several similar-looking gully and bench variations that do not all go
A small summit area with a steeply inclined south slab whose slip line runs down the east face
Lingering snow and possible cornices in the summit gullies through June
A dry approach above the valley bottom, with the last easy water a quarter mile past the trail's end
Unmaintained, log-choked trail sections from past wildfire damage on the lower six miles

approach_variants.name: North Fork Entiat and the primitive Pyramid Creek Trail to the Emerald-Saska basin
approach_variants.season: Mid-Jul-Sep once the col and summit gullies clear. October adds larch colour and early-snow risk; before mid-July carry an axe for lingering snow and ice
approach_variants.notes:
From the North Fork Entiat Trailhead near 3,880-3,940 ft at the end of FR-5606, the first four miles of Trail #1437 climb gently up the valley through old burn, where blowdown and washed-out sections make the going slower than the grade suggests. There is little shade and the valley bottom runs hot and dry — carry water.

Continue up-valley another four miles, gaining roughly 3,000 ft from the trailhead, to the Pyramid Creek / Fern Lake junction. Sources put that junction anywhere from seven to nine miles in depending on how far up the road you were able to start. Fox Camp sits about a quarter mile north of it.

From the junction take the primitive, unmaintained Pyramid Creek Trail EAST and climb about 1,000 ft over a mile to a mile and a half into the upper basin between Emerald and Saska, around 7,100 ft. The tread is intermittent. Pushing to that camp rather than stopping at the junction costs an extra hour on the approach day and returns about the same on summit day.

This is reported as the easiest and shortest of the Saska / Emerald / Cardinal trio's summit scrambles.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE COL AND THE DIRECTION OFF IT IS WEST. From the basin camp, about 600 ft of gain on talus, scree or lingering snow reaches the EMERALD-SASKA COL at roughly 7,700 ft — a notch on the south ridge with a peak on either side. From the col, HEAD WEST toward Saska. Emerald is the other way. If you leave the col climbing east you are on the neighbouring peak's ground.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS THAT YOU DO NOT STAY ON THE CREST. The connecting ridge is narrow and knife-edged in places with steep drop-offs on both sides, so the usual line DROPS SLIGHTLY ONTO ITS WEST FLANK to pick up an OBVIOUS SCREE-AND-ROCK GULLY, then follows a CAIRNED RISING TRAVERSE back toward the crest. West flank, gully, cairned rising traverse. A party grimly balancing along the crest itself has missed the line rather than found the hard way.

THE FINISH IS COUNTED IN FEET, NOT FEATURES: roughly 300 ft of final Class 3 on loose blocks gains the top. Test every hold — nothing here is fixed and no rope is standard, although the last exposed moves are steep enough that some parties carry a short handline for them.

THE DESCENT MARKER IS A WARNING WITH A DOCUMENTED CONSEQUENCE: CLIFF BANDS SIT BELOW THE SOUTH-WEST FACE. Stay well clear of them when the ground is snow-covered or icy. A winter party misjudging that descent line in icy conditions lost a ski over those cliffs. In early-to-mid season the continuous snow below the col gives a glissade or boot-ski; by August and September the same ground is loose scree and dirt that has to be walked slowly.

LOOSE ROCK IS THE THEME OF THE WHOLE CIRQUE. Helmet, and do not stack the party directly above one another, from the moment you leave the basin.
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall throughout the Emerald-Saska col basin and along the summit ridge
Cliff bands below the south-west face that have caught descending parties in icy or snow-covered conditions
A narrow, sometimes knife-edged connecting crest that has to be avoided rather than followed
Lingering snow and ice in the col and summit gullies into early-to-mid July in heavy years
Heavy blowdown and washed-out sections on the lower North Fork Entiat Trail from past wildfires and storm damage

_SKIPPED._note: Six routes with an empty approach_variants were deliberately left empty. An empty result is a real result; each reason is a statement about what is published or about what the row is, not about effort.
_SKIPPED.wa_bonanza_peak_north_ridge: CONTAMINATED ROW, AND THE CONTAMINATION IS IN THE FIELD THAT WOULD HAVE SUPPLIED THE BASE. Its beta reads 'From the Middle Fork Snoqualmie trailhead, approach via the alpine meadows to the north ridge base' — the Middle Fork Snoqualmie is roughly 120 km away across the Cascade crest and has no route to Bonanza Peak. Its grade is 'Class 2' on a peak whose standard route is Class 5.0-5.6 and whose every other line is Grade V. And its approach and pitch_detail describe the Mary Green Glacier's north edge and the upper rock band to a notch on the NE ridge, which is the STANDARD route's own upper section, already written on wa_bonanza_peak_mary_green_glacier. Writing a base here would mean either repeating the standard route's base finding under a different name or inventing one for a line nothing independently describes.
_SKIPPED.wa_cardinal_peak_nw_couloir_north_ridge: POSITIONED ONLY RELATIVE TO ITS NEIGHBOURS, AND EMPTY OF EVERYTHING ELSE. The row carries no gain_ft, no dist_km, no high_point_ft and no length_m. Its whole approach is 'reached via the North Fork Entiat Trail to Saska Basin and Saska Pass, commonly combined with ascents of Saska Peak, Emerald Peak and Pinnacle Mountain on the same trip rather than as a dedicated single-peak approach', and its only locating claim is 'climbs a couloir on the northwest side to gain the north ridge'. The neighbouring Southeast Slopes row already describes a north-west-FACING gully on the same flank leading to the notch between the north and middle summits, so 'a couloir on the northwest side' does not separate the two. Every published account of this ridge is of parties ABANDONING it for snow and verglas and traversing onto the south-east slopes to finish — which is the other route.
_SKIPPED.wa_fortress_mountain_northeast_face: NO INDEPENDENT BASE, BY THE ROW'S OWN ACCOUNT. Its approach column says in as many words that this line 'is normally climbed or descended as part of a link-up with the East Ridge or Southwest Slope rather than approached independently', and its beta says very little beta exists online beyond a single forum report. The one concrete marker it holds — a fourth-class chimney that a party missed near an 8,500 ft col — is a DESCENT-finding note about a feature partway up the ridge, not the base of the climb. The row's id says northeast_face, its name says Northeast Ridge and its face field says both; see _DEFECTS.
_SKIPPED.wa_emerald_peak_west_route: APPARENT DUPLICATE. wa_emerald_peak_west_route and wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge carry the SAME high_point_ft (8,422) and the SAME gain_ft (5,272), start from the same North Fork Entiat trailhead, and both describe climbing a scree gully to the summit block and finishing with a short Class 3 scramble on a summit split into two points about 100 ft apart with the north one true. The one substantive difference is that the West Route names an alternate approach by boat to Lucerne and the Emerald Park Trail, and nothing published says where on that trail you leave it for the peak's west flank. The SE Ridge row is the one written — it carries waypoints, a documented basin camp and the drainage line that leads into the upper basin. Writing both would put two base findings on what is probably one gully.
_SKIPPED.wa_mount_pugh_pika_slab: THE ROW ITSELF SAYS THE LOCATION IS NOT PUBLISHED. Its beta records that the peak's area page 'describes an abundance of small crags immediately above the trail between Stujack Pass and the summit, of which Pika Slab is the one named route' and that 'detailed pitch-by-pitch beta, first-ascent info, and exact location are not published'. So the band is unmistakable — you walk through it — and the individual slab is not distinguishable from its neighbours by anything anyone has written down. Twenty feet of white slab above a trail, somewhere past a Class 3 rock step, is a description of the crag band rather than a test for this route. The approach itself is fully covered by wa_mount_pugh_stujack, which shares every foot of it.
_SKIPPED.wa_don_t_climb_that_she_said: NO PUBLISHED APPROACH EXISTS AND THE ROW SAYS SO. Its approach column records that no route-specific trailhead or approach beta turned up in any guidebook, forum or trip-report source, and that the name reads like a locally-known label rather than a catalogued line. Everything else in that column is explicitly INFERRED from the row's own numbers ('based on the on-file numbers … expect an informal boot-path'). There is nothing to re-home and nothing to research. It is also almost certainly misfiled; see _DEFECTS.

_DEFECTS._note: Data defects noticed in passing while reading these rows. Reported, not fixed — this batch writes only approach_variants.
_DEFECTS.bonanza_north_ridge_beta_is_from_another: wa_bonanza_peak_north_ridge's beta begins 'From the Middle Fork Snoqualmie trailhead, approach via the alpine meadows to the north ridge base. Follow the ridge crest, staying on solid rock and stable talus. Most routefinding is straightforward and well-marked by cairns.' The Middle Fork Snoqualmie is on the west side of the Cascade crest roughly 120 km from Bonanza and no approach connects them; Bonanza has no drivable trailhead at all. The row's grade is also 'Class 2' where the peak's standard route is Class 5.0-5.6. Two independent contamination signals on one row.
_DEFECTS.bonanza_west_ridge_beta_describes_volcan: wa_bonanza_peak_west_ridge's beta says the ridge 'becomes steeper above 8,000 ft with Class 2-3 scrambling on red volcanic rock'. Bonanza is meta-granitic orthogneiss — wa_soviet_route's own beta says so, and describes bands of loose RED rock within it, which is probably where the word came from. Nothing else on this peak supports a Class 2-3 scramble line on the west ridge: the Soviet's descent off the West Peak needs two roughly 200 ft rappels down slabs. The row's approach column (Hart Lake to the 7,100 ft North Star-Bonanza pass) is correct and is what the variant written here covers.
_DEFECTS.bonanza_northeast_buttress_contradicts_i: wa_bonanza_peak_northeast_buttress carries gain_ft 6,300 while its own approach prose explains 'this route's noticeably larger overall gain (~7,500')'. The column and the sentence beside it disagree by 1,200 ft. Its summit waypoint also reads 9,516 ft against a high_point_ft of 9,511.
_DEFECTS.bonanza_rows_disagree_on_holden_pass: Holden Pass is given as 6,360 ft in wa_bonanza_peak_north_ridge and wa_bonanza_peak_northeast_buttress's approach prose, and as 6,400 ft in the waypoint and bivy records on the same rows. Small, but it is the high camp for three routes and two peaks.
_DEFECTS.cascadian_gain_ft_is_route_vertical_not_: wa_bonanza_peak_cascadian_route carries gain_ft 2,000, which is the route's own vertical gain as published, while every sibling row on this peak uses gain_ft for the whole day from the trailhead (wa_soviet_route 5,300, wa_bonanza_peak_northeast_buttress 6,300). One column, two conventions, on one peak.
_DEFECTS.kololo_disagrees_with_itself_on_which_su: wa_kololo_peaks_standard's beta says the east summit at 8,243 ft is the true high point and the west is 8,220 ft. Its pitch_detail says 'Kololo Peaks has twin summits (an east summit near 8,160+ ft and the higher west/main summit)'. Its high_point_ft is 8,240 and its summit waypoint is named 'Kololo Peaks (west summit)' at 8,240. Three different answers to which top is higher, inside one row. wa_tenpeak_mountain_north_couloir independently calls Kololo 8,220 ft.
_DEFECTS.kololo_distance_prose_contradicts_the_co: wa_kololo_peaks_standard's approach prose says 'the on-file 46.99 km distance reflects a round trip in the 28-29 mile range' while the row's dist_km is 22.9. The prose is describing a number the row does not hold.
_DEFECTS.tenpeak_thunder_basin_camp_has_three_ele: wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast puts the standard Thunder Basin high camp at '~5,180 ft' in its approach prose and again at 5,180 in its beta, at 6,400 ft in its 'Thunder Basin high camp' waypoint, and at 6,200 ft in the shared bivy record ('Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River'). Over a thousand feet of disagreement about where to sleep.
_DEFECTS.copper_peak_name_and_aspect_disagree_wit: wa_copper_peak_south_route is named the South Route with aspect SE, while its climbing_route, pitch_detail and every waypoint describe the EAST-facing Southeast Glacier remnant, a gully breaching the spur on the ridge's NORTH side, and the upper NORTHEAST Ridge to the summit. Its face field says 'Southeast Glacier/Face'. Navigating this route by its name or its aspect column would send a party to the wrong side of the peak.
_DEFECTS.fortress_northeast_row_has_three_names_f: wa_fortress_mountain_northeast_face has id ...northeast_face, name 'Northeast Ridge', and face 'Northeast Face/Ridge (Fortress-Chiwawa saddle)'. Its own beta says the line 'is inaccurately described in Beckey's most recent Cascade Alpine Guide', so the ambiguity is not only ours. Separately its access.closures reads only 'Access road unplowed in winter' while both sibling rows on the same peak carry the FR-6200 storm closure beyond Atkinson Flat — stale bookkeeping on one row of three.
_DEFECTS.fortress_rows_lose_more_than_they_gain: wa_fortress_mountain_east_ridge carries gain_ft 5,884 and loss_ft 7,900; wa_fortress_mountain_southwest_face carries gain_ft 5,884 and loss_ft 6,000.
